articles.title: Best Regulated Crypto Exchanges in the US
articles.description: Not a ranked list — a guide to how to check registration and regulatory status yourself, so you're not relying on anyone else's opinion.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

Why we won't rank exchanges for you

You'll find many articles online titled something like "Top 10 Best Crypto Exchanges," often ranking specific platforms with star ratings. Many of these lists are funded by affiliate commissions or paid placements from the very companies being ranked, which is a genuine conflict of interest, even when it's disclosed only in fine print.

We think you're better served by learning to check a platform's actual regulatory status yourself, using free, public, official sources. That knowledge works for any exchange, today or one that launches five years from now, and it doesn't depend on trusting our opinion or anyone else's.

The layers of US regulation that can apply

Unlike a single national system, crypto platforms serving US customers can be subject to several separate, overlapping types of oversight:

WHO REGULATES WHAT
Regulator What it covers
FinCEN (federal) Anti-money laundering and Bank Secrecy Act compliance for money services businesses
State money transmitter regulators State-by-state licensing to legally transmit money, including crypto, in that state
NYDFS (New York specifically) A separate, notably strict "BitLicense" for virtual currency business activity
SEC Oversight of any offerings or products that may qualify as securities
CFTC Oversight of commodity and derivatives-related products, including some crypto derivatives
OCC (federal) Bank and trust charters, relevant to platforms pursuing a national trust bank structure

A platform can be properly registered with FinCEN and hold state money transmitter licenses without being registered with the SEC or CFTC, because those apply to different kinds of activity. Don't assume one type of registration covers everything.

How to check any exchange, step by step

  1. Search FinCEN's MSB Registrant Search (fincen.gov) for the company's legal name to confirm federal money services business registration.
  2. Search NMLS Consumer Access (nmlsconsumeraccess.org) to check state-level money transmitter licenses.
  3. If the platform is based in or serves New York specifically, check NYDFS's public list of licensed virtual currency businesses.
  4. If the platform offers products that resemble securities or derivatives, check the SEC's EDGAR database and the CFTC/NFA BASIC lookup.
  5. Read the platform's own legal and licensing disclosure pages, which US-facing exchanges are generally required to publish, and cross-check the specific license numbers listed against the official databases above rather than taking the list at face value.
  6. Search for regulatory actions or warnings from state securities regulators, the SEC, the CFTC, or the FTC involving that company's name.

A worked example of the process

Is Coinbase Regulated? walks through exactly this process applied to one specific, commonly searched platform: what it's registered for, what it isn't, and how each piece was verified. Use that as a template for checking any exchange you're considering, rather than treating it as a specific recommendation.

Beyond registration: other questions worth asking

Registration is a floor, not a ceiling. Even among properly registered platforms, it's worth comparing:

  • How clearly fees are disclosed before you trade.
  • What happens to customer assets if the company fails, and whether that's explained in plain language.
  • How responsive support actually is, based on independent user reports, not the company's own marketing.
  • Whether withdrawals work smoothly in a small test, as covered in Is This Exchange Legit?

Keep in mind

  • Registration reduces certain risks, but doesn't eliminate them. Regulated companies can still fail, be mismanaged, or be hacked.
  • Regulatory status can change, so re-check periodically rather than assuming a one-time search stays accurate forever.
  • We do not rank, rate, or recommend specific exchanges, here or anywhere else on this site. This guide gives you the method, not a conclusion.

articles.title: Fake Exchange Warning Signs
articles.description: How to tell a real exchange website from a convincing fake one before you ever type in your password.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

How fake exchanges work

A fake exchange is a website or app built to look like a real trading platform, or like a well-known one. There are two common versions:

  • The clone. A copy of a real platform's login page, built to capture your username, password, and sometimes your recovery phrase.
  • The invented platform. A brand-new "exchange" that shows fake balances and gains, then blocks withdrawals or demands extra payments.

Both look professional. Design tells you nothing about legitimacy.

How people end up there

  • Sponsored search results. Scam sites can appear as ads above the real result.
  • Social media ads and comments, often with fake testimonials.
  • Messages and emails with urgent "security alert" links.
  • Referrals from strangers or online "friends."
  • Fake apps in app stores or installed from a link outside the official store.

Check the address carefully

  • Look for tiny differences: swapped or extra letters, added words like "secure" or "login," or hyphens.
  • Look at the ending, such as unusual domain endings that don't match the company's real one.
  • Don't treat the padlock as proof. A padlock only means the connection is encrypted. Scammers get them too.
  • Check how new the domain is. A free "domain lookup" tool can show its registration date. A platform claiming years of history on a domain registered weeks ago is a red flag.
  • Bookmark the real site after finding it once through a trusted source, and use only that bookmark.
A handy tip

Password managers usually autofill only on the exact website where you saved a login. If yours doesn't offer to fill in your password, stop and check the address.

Check the app too

  • Download only from your phone's official app store, using the link from the company's real website.
  • Check the publisher name, number of downloads, and review history. A new app with few downloads and glowing reviews is suspicious.
  • Never install an app by tapping a link or file sent to you by a stranger.
  • Be very cautious with any app you were told to use by someone you met online.

Behavior that gives a fake platform away

SIDE BY SIDE
Real platform Fake platform
Explains fees clearly and up front Surprise "taxes," "unlock fees," or "verification deposits" to withdraw
Doesn't promise returns Guaranteed profits, deposit bonuses, "VIP" tiers
Support available through official site channels Support only through private chat apps, or someone contacting you first
Deposits go to addresses shown inside your own logged-in account Asked to send money to a personal wallet or an individual's account
Withdrawals work in a small test Small withdrawals work, then larger ones are blocked
Verifiable company and registration No verifiable company, or claims you can't check

A two-minute check before you log in

  1. Did I get here from my own bookmark or by typing the address?
  2. Does the address match the real one, letter for letter?
  3. Does my password manager recognize the site?
  4. Have I verified the company through these steps?
  5. Am I being rushed by anyone?

If you already entered your details

  • If you typed only a password: change it right away from a trusted device, change it anywhere else you used it, and turn on 2FA. See Two-Factor Authentication, Explained.
  • If you entered a recovery phrase: assume that wallet is compromised. Create a new wallet with a new phrase and move any remaining funds immediately.
  • If you deposited money: stop, don't pay "fees," and keep records.
  • Report it to the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov) and the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov), then read How to Recover Stolen Crypto.

Keep in mind

  • Fakes improve constantly, so no single sign is decisive.
  • A real address can be spoofed in messages and ads, so navigate yourself.
  • Speed is on the scammers' side. Slowing down is the best defense.

articles.title: Self-Custody vs. Exchange Custody
articles.description: What actually happens to your coins in each case, the trade-offs of both, and how to decide which fits you.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What "custody" actually means

As covered in How Does Cryptocurrency Actually Work?, owning crypto really means controlling the private key that authorizes spending it. Custody is simply the question of who holds that key.

There are two basic arrangements: you hold it yourself (self-custody), or a company holds it on your behalf (exchange, or third-party custody). Everything else in this guide follows from that one difference.

How exchange custody works

When you buy crypto on most exchanges and simply leave it there, the exchange holds the actual private keys in its own systems. Your account shows a balance, similar to how a bank app shows your balance, but the underlying assets sit in the exchange's infrastructure, not in a wallet only you control.

This is convenient. There's no recovery phrase for you to protect, password resets are possible, and moving funds is usually as easy as using a banking app. The trade-off is that you're trusting the company's security, honesty, and financial stability.

How self-custody works

With self-custody, you hold the private keys yourself, typically using a software or hardware wallet as covered in Crypto Wallets for Beginners. No company sits between you and your funds.

This gives you direct control, and it removes the risk of an exchange failing or freezing your account. It also removes the safety net: there's no password reset, and no company to call if you make a mistake or lose your keys.

Side by side

COMPARISON
Exchange custody Self-custody
Who holds the keys The exchange You
If you forget your password Usually recoverable through support Recoverable only if you have your own backup
If the company fails or is hacked Your funds may be delayed, reduced, or lost, depending on the case Not affected by that company at all
If you make a sending mistake Support may sometimes help, depending on the situation Usually final, with no company to appeal to
Insurance Not FDIC-insured; some platforms carry limited private insurance with specific conditions No equivalent protection; security is entirely your responsibility
Convenience High; similar to online banking Lower; you manage your own security

Why the difference isn't just theoretical

This isn't a hypothetical trade-off. Several major exchanges and lending platforms have collapsed, including FTX and Celsius in 2022, leaving customers unable to access funds that had been held in those companies' custody, with recovery processes that dragged on for years through bankruptcy court and, in some cases, resulted in customers recovering only a portion of what they had deposited.

Worth knowing

Crypto held on an exchange is generally treated as an unsecured claim against that company if it goes bankrupt, similar to how other creditors are treated, not as your own separately protected property the way it would be in true self-custody.

How to decide what fits you

Neither option is universally correct. Some honest questions to weigh:

  • How much am I holding? Many people use exchange custody for smaller or frequently traded amounts, and consider self-custody as the amount grows.
  • Am I actively trading, or holding long-term? Frequent trading is far more convenient with exchange custody.
  • Am I confident I can manage a recovery phrase responsibly? Self-custody has zero safety net if you lose it.
  • How much do I trust this specific platform? See Is This Exchange Legit? before leaving any meaningful amount with one.
  • Could I still function if this exchange froze my account tomorrow? If the answer is no, that's worth taking seriously.

Some people use both: keeping an amount they're actively trading on an exchange, while moving long-term holdings into self-custody. That's a reasonable middle ground, not a rule.

Risks to understand

  • Exchange custody risk: company failure, hacks, mismanagement, or fraud can all result in loss of funds that are legally and practically outside your direct control.
  • Self-custody risk: a lost recovery phrase or a compromised device can mean permanent, unrecoverable loss, with no company to appeal to.
  • No option is risk-free. Choosing between them means choosing which specific risks you're more prepared to manage, not eliminating risk altogether.

articles.title: How Much Money Do You Need to Start?
articles.description: Spoiler: much less than people think. This guide covers realistic starting amounts and why bigger isn't automatically better.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The short answer

There's no official minimum to own crypto. You don't need thousands of dollars, and you don't need to buy a whole coin.

The more useful question isn't "what's the minimum?" It's "what's an amount I can afford to lose completely without it hurting my life?" That number is personal, and it's usually smaller than beginners expect.

You can buy a small piece

Cryptocurrencies are divisible. You can own a tiny fraction of one Bitcoin, or of most other coins. So a high price per coin does not mean you need a large amount to take part.

Many platforms let you buy in small dollar amounts, but the minimum varies by platform and can change, so check the current rules and fees on whichever service you use rather than assuming.

Before your first dollar: check the foundation

Crypto is a high-risk, speculative asset. Most financial educators suggest getting the basics in order first:

  1. Emergency fund. Have some savings set aside for unexpected costs, so you never have to sell in a hurry.
  2. High-interest debt. Credit card interest is often higher than any return you could reasonably expect. Paying it down is a guaranteed "return."
  3. Short-term money. Don't use money you'll need in the next few years, such as rent, tuition, or a house deposit.
  4. Never borrow to invest. Not on credit cards, not on loans, not on margin.

The sleep-well test

A simple check

Imagine the amount you're considering goes to zero tomorrow. If that would cause real stress, force you to skip bills, or change your plans, it's too much for now. Cut it until the answer feels calm.

This isn't pessimism. Crypto assets have fallen by more than half several times, and some have gone to near zero. Deciding your maximum loss in advance makes it easier to stay level-headed when prices move.

Why very small purchases can be surprisingly expensive

Fees are often a fixed amount plus a percentage, so a small purchase can lose a big share to costs. Here's a hypothetical to show the effect:

HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE
Purchase Hypothetical flat fee Fee as share of purchase
$20 $2 10%
$100 $2 2%
$500 $2 0.4%
Illustrative numbers only. Real fees vary widely by platform, payment method, and order type.

So "start tiny" has a floor. Before buying, look at the full fee structure, including spreads, deposit fees, and withdrawal fees, and consider a size where costs don't swallow much of the purchase.

Why bigger isn't automatically better

  • You're still learning. Early mistakes, like wrong addresses, phishing, and unfamiliar apps, cost less when the amount is small.
  • Big amounts create big emotions. Larger sums make it harder to think clearly during a drop.
  • You can always add later. Starting small doesn't lock you out. It just lets you build experience first.
  • Concentration risk. Putting a large share of your savings into one volatile asset means one bad outcome can hurt your whole plan.

Thinking about size in the bigger picture

Many financial advisors treat speculative assets as a small slice of a diversified portfolio, not the foundation of it. What counts as "small" depends on your income, savings, goals, and age, which is why this guide can't give you a number.

A licensed financial advisor can help you decide, based on your actual situation.

A cautious way to begin, if you decide to

  1. Read the basics first, including What Is Bitcoin, Really? and Crypto Wallets for Beginners.
  2. Decide the maximum amount you're willing to lose, and write it down.
  3. Choose a reputable, regulated platform and read its fee schedule.
  4. Turn on two-factor authentication before depositing anything.
  5. Start with an amount well under your maximum, and consider whether spreading it out makes sense. See Dollar-Cost Averaging.
  6. Keep records of every purchase, since they matter at tax time.

Risks to understand

  • You can lose all of it. That's the honest worst case, and it's why the amount matters.
  • Fees can be disproportionate on small trades.
  • No safety net: crypto isn't covered by bank-style deposit insurance.
  • Scams often target beginners with promises tied to deposit size.
  • Rules and taxes apply even to small amounts.

articles.title: How to Spot a Crypto Scam
articles.description: The core warning signs — guaranteed returns, pressure to act fast, secrecy — explained with real examples of how scams actually present themselves.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

Why this matters

Crypto scams are not rare. According to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center, Americans filed more than 181,000 cryptocurrency-related complaints in 2025, with reported losses of roughly $11 billion. Those are only the losses people reported, and the real total is likely higher.

The takeaway isn't to be afraid of crypto. It's that scammers go where money and confusion meet, and beginners are their favorite audience.

The one thing every scam has in common

Scams rarely depend on clever technology. They depend on emotion: greed ("you'll double your money"), fear ("your account is compromised"), urgency ("only today"), and trust ("I'm your friend"). Once you're feeling one of those strongly, you're less likely to check facts.

A useful habit

When something makes you feel rushed, excited, or scared about money, treat that feeling itself as the warning sign. Slow down first, then verify.

The core warning signs

  1. Guaranteed or unusually high returns. No legitimate investment can guarantee profit. Promises of fixed daily or weekly gains are the most reliable sign of fraud.
  2. Pressure to act fast. Countdown timers, "limited spots," and "last chance" messaging exist to stop you from thinking.
  3. Secrecy. Being told not to tell family, your bank, or friends is a major red flag. Honest opportunities can survive questions.
  4. Unsolicited contact. Out-of-the-blue messages, wrong-number texts that turn friendly, or "advisors" who find you on social media.
  5. Payment only in crypto, gift cards, or cash at a kiosk. These are chosen because they're hard to reverse and trace.
  6. Requests for your recovery phrase or passwords. No genuine service ever needs them.
  7. Fees to withdraw. If you're told you must pay a "tax," "unlock fee," or "verification deposit" to get your own money out, it's a scam.
  8. Celebrity or "insider" endorsements. Famous faces and voices are easy to fake, and hacked accounts make fake posts look official.

How scams actually present themselves

Scams change costume constantly, but the patterns repeat. Here's what some of the most common ones look like from the victim's side:

COMMON PATTERNS
What it looks like What's really happening
A stranger contacts you by mistake, becomes a friendly presence, and eventually mentions an investing platform A long-running confidence scheme. See What Is a "Pig Butchering" Scam?
An ad or video with a famous person promoting a trading system or a "giveaway" Impersonation or a fake endorsement. See Crypto Giveaway Scams
A polished app or website showing your balance growing, but withdrawals stall A fake platform. See Fake Exchange Warning Signs
A new token with heavy hype that suddenly collapses See Crypto Rug Pull, Meaning
A call, text, or pop-up claiming to be your bank, a government agency, or "support," telling you to move money into crypto for safety An impersonation scam. Real institutions never ask you to do this

A note on crypto ATMs

Crypto ATMs (kiosks that turn cash into crypto) are now a common tool in scams. In its 2025 report, the FBI noted that reported losses from crypto ATM and kiosk scams climbed to hundreds of millions of dollars.

Per FTC guidance, no legitimate business or government agency will demand payment in cryptocurrency or tell you to deposit cash into a crypto ATM. If anyone is on the phone pushing you toward a kiosk, hang up.

A two-minute pause checklist

  1. Who contacted whom? If they contacted you first, be extra careful.
  2. Am I being rushed, or told to keep this quiet?
  3. Am I being asked to pay in a way that can't be reversed?
  4. Can I verify this company or person independently, using a source I found myself?
  5. Would I be comfortable explaining this to a trusted friend or family member?

If any answer worries you, stop. You lose nothing by waiting, and a real opportunity will still be there tomorrow.

What to do if something feels wrong

  • Stop. Don't send more money or share any codes or phrases.
  • Don't argue with them. Just stop replying.
  • Keep evidence: screenshots, usernames, wallet addresses, links, and transaction IDs.
  • Report it to the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov) and the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov).
If you've already sent money

Stop sending anything further, keep every record, and read How to Recover Stolen Crypto for the exact steps and the agencies to contact. Acting quickly can matter.

Keep in mind

  • Legitimate projects can still lose you money. Not every loss is a scam, and crypto prices are volatile.
  • Scammers adapt. A checklist helps, but judgment and patience matter most.
  • Reporting is worth doing even if you don't expect to get money back, because it helps investigators connect cases.

articles.title: What Is DeFi in Crypto?
articles.description: “Decentralized finance” explained without the buzzwords — and how its risks differ from traditional banking.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What DeFi means

DeFi is short for "decentralized finance." It refers to financial services, like lending, borrowing, and trading, built using smart contracts on a blockchain instead of being run by a bank or brokerage.

Instead of applying for a loan through a bank's staff and systems, a DeFi lending platform uses code that automatically manages deposits, loans, and interest, based on rules anyone can inspect.

How it generally works

Most DeFi activity revolves around a few core building blocks:

  • Lending and borrowing platforms: people deposit crypto to earn interest, while others borrow against collateral they've deposited.
  • Decentralized exchanges (DEXs): let people trade one token for another directly through smart contracts, without a company holding their funds in the middle.
  • Liquidity pools: pools of tokens that users contribute to, which DEXs and other platforms use to enable trading. Contributors can earn a share of fees, but also take on specific risks covered below.
  • Yield strategies: ways of moving funds between different DeFi platforms to try to earn a return, often layering several of the tools above together.

How this differs from a traditional bank

SIDE BY SIDE
Traditional banking DeFi
A company holds your money and manages the system Smart contract code manages the system; often no single company is fully in control
Deposits are FDIC-insured up to a limit No government deposit insurance
Customer service can review and reverse some errors Transactions are generally final; no customer service to appeal to
Access can require an application or credit check Often open to anyone with a compatible wallet
Interest rates set by the institution, often published and steady Rates can change quickly based on supply, demand, and token incentives

Why people are drawn to it

  • Open access, without needing approval from a bank.
  • Transparency, since the code and, often, the transactions are publicly viewable.
  • Potentially higher yields than traditional savings products, though higher yield generally reflects higher risk, not a free bonus.
  • No intermediary fees to a company in the traditional sense, though network and protocol fees still apply.

Risks that work differently than in traditional banking

  • Smart contract bugs. If the underlying code has a flaw, funds can be stolen or lost, sometimes very quickly and at large scale.
  • No deposit insurance. Unlike a bank account, there's no FDIC-style backstop if a platform fails or is exploited.
  • Impermanent loss. Contributing to a liquidity pool can result in ending up with less value than simply holding the original tokens, depending on how their prices move relative to each other. This is a real, well-documented risk specific to liquidity pools, not a bug.
  • Flash loan exploits. Some attacks use very large, instant loans, borrowed and repaid within a single transaction, to manipulate a platform's pricing and drain funds. This is a technical attack specific to DeFi's design.
  • Governance risk. Some platforms let token holders vote on changes, which can occasionally be exploited if voting power becomes concentrated.
  • Irreversible mistakes. Sending funds to the wrong contract or approving the wrong permission usually can't be undone.
  • Regulatory uncertainty. Rules for DeFi are still developing and could change how platforms operate or who can access them.
Common mistake

Assuming a high advertised yield is simply "free money." Unusually high returns in DeFi typically reflect unusually high risk, whether from an unstable token, a temporary incentive, or the underlying platform itself.

A cautious way to think about DeFi

  • Understand that DeFi is generally more technical and more experimental than most other parts of crypto covered in this hub.
  • Only use amounts you could fully afford to lose, given the added smart-contract and platform risks.
  • Look for platforms that have been reviewed by independent security researchers, while remembering that a security review reduces, but never eliminates, risk.
  • Be especially skeptical of new platforms promising unusually high yields with little explanation of where that yield actually comes from.

articles.title: Is This Exchange Legit?
articles.description: A step-by-step way to check whether a platform is actually registered and trustworthy before you deposit money.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

An honest starting point

No checklist can prove a platform is safe. But most losses to fake or fraudulent platforms could be avoided with a few basic checks, done before you deposit anything.

Also remember that even well-known, professional-looking platforms can collapse. Several large ones have, including FTX in 2022. A polished brand is never proof of safety.

Eight checks, in order

  1. Identify the company. Look for a legal company name, a physical address, named leadership with real track records, and how long it has operated. Vague or hidden details are a red flag.
  2. Check U.S. registration. Platforms serving U.S. customers generally must register as money services businesses with FinCEN, and many also need state licenses. Use FinCEN's MSB registrant search and NMLS Consumer Access, and check your state regulator's list.
  3. Check for other regulators if relevant. If a platform offers securities, use FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC. For derivatives, check the CFTC and NFA BASIC lookup.
  4. Look at regulator warning lists. State securities regulators, the CFTC, and the FTC publish alerts about fraudulent platforms.
  5. Read what's said about custody and insurance. Crypto is not FDIC-insured. Be wary of vague claims about "insured" funds, and read exactly what any insurance covers.
  6. Research reputation carefully. Search the platform's name with words like "withdrawal problems" or "complaints." Beware of fake reviews and paid "best exchange" rankings.
  7. Verify the real web address and app. See Fake Exchange Warning Signs.
  8. Test small first. Deposit a small amount, then make a withdrawal, before moving anything larger.

Green flags and red flags

QUICK COMPARISON
Reassuring signs Warning signs
Clear legal entity, address, and named leadership Anonymous company, no address, no named team
Appears in official registration databases Can't be found in any registry, or gives a registration number that doesn't check out
Clear fee schedule and terms Unclear fees, or "fees" appear only when you try to withdraw
Withdrawals work smoothly in a small test Withdrawals delayed, blocked, or tied to extra payments
No promises of returns Guaranteed returns, deposit bonuses, or "VIP" levels
Support through official channels on the real site Support only through private chat apps, or contacts you first

Common mistakes

  • Trusting a registration number the platform gives you without looking it up yourself in the official database.
  • Assuming a foreign platform must be licensed in the U.S. Some serve U.S. users without proper authorization.
  • Relying on social media proof like screenshots of withdrawals, which are easy to fake.
  • Judging by design. Professional-looking sites are cheap to build.

If you're still unsure

Then don't deposit. There will always be another platform, and waiting costs you nothing. If you were pointed to a platform by someone you met online, read What Is a "Pig Butchering" Scam? before going any further.

Keep in mind

  • Registration isn't a safety guarantee, only a baseline.
  • Funds on an exchange are an obligation of that company, not protected like a bank deposit.
  • Rules change. Always check current information on the regulators' own sites.

What dollar-cost averaging is

Dollar-cost averaging (often shortened to DCA) means investing a fixed amount of money at regular intervals, regardless of the price. For example, $50 every week, or $200 on the first of each month.

Instead of trying to pick the perfect moment for one big purchase, you spread your buying over time. When the price is lower, your fixed amount buys more units. When it's higher, it buys fewer.

Average cost per unit: $400 ÷ 10.5 ≈ $38.10. The simple average of the four prices is $41.25. If the price ends at $50, the holding is worth about $525.

Notice what happened: because more units were bought when the price was low, the average cost came out below the simple average price. That's the effect people are referring to when they talk about "averaging."

The important lesson

DCA lowered the average cost in both scenarios, but in Scenario B the investor still lost money. DCA is a way of buying, not a protection against a falling asset.

What DCA can help with

  • Removing the timing pressure. You don't have to guess the "right" day.

  • Reducing regret. If a big single purchase is followed by a drop, it can feel awful. Smaller regular buys soften that feeling.

  • Building a habit. A schedule keeps decisions calm and consistent instead of emotional.

  • Easing in. It lets you get used to volatility with less at stake at any one moment.

What DCA does not do

  • It doesn't guarantee a profit or prevent losses, as Scenario B showed.

  • It doesn't make a weak asset strong. If the asset itself fails, regular buying just means more money into it.

  • It isn't always better than a lump sum. Research on traditional stock markets, including work by Vanguard, has found that investing a lump sum immediately has often come out ahead of spreading purchases, because markets have tended to rise more often than fall over time. Crypto is different and far more volatile, so those results can't simply be assumed to carry over. The real benefit of DCA is usually psychological, not mathematical.

Honest summary

DCA is a risk-management and behavior tool. It can make investing feel more manageable, but it's not a strategy for beating the market.

How people typically set it up

  1. Decide an amount you can afford to lose. See How Much Money Do You Need to Start?

  2. Pick a schedule you can keep up: weekly, every two weeks, or monthly.

  3. Check the fees. Many small purchases can add up. Compare per-purchase costs on your platform.

  4. Consider automation. Some platforms offer recurring purchases. Check the current options and their fees.

  5. Keep records. Every purchase is a separate transaction with its own cost basis, which matters for taxes. See our US Taxes section.

  6. Review occasionally, not constantly. Checking prices every hour defeats the calming purpose.

Common mistakes

  • Stopping when the price falls. Pausing during a dip is understandable, but it undermines the whole idea of a steady plan.

  • Increasing the amount during hype. Buying more because everything is rising is FOMO, not a plan.

  • Ignoring fees on very small, frequent purchases.

  • Using money you'll need soon. A schedule doesn't change the risk of a volatile asset.

  • Treating it as safe. A plan can feel safe without the underlying asset being safe.

Who it might suit, and who it might not

It may suit people who are new, who feel anxious about timing, and who have regular income to invest gradually. It may not add much if you already have a clear, well-considered plan, or if you're uncomfortable with the asset itself. Neither choice is wrong, and a licensed financial advisor can help you decide.

Risks to understand

  • The asset can still fall, and you can lose some or all of what you invest.

  • Fees can accumulate across many small purchases.

  • Tax recordkeeping grows with every additional purchase.

  • Discipline is the hard part. The method only works as a habit if you actually keep to it.

  • Scams exploit this too. Beware "automatic investing" services that ask you to send money to unfamiliar accounts or promise returns.

articles.title: How Is Cryptocurrency Taxed in the US?
articles.description: The core rules explained plainly — what counts as a taxable event, and how capital gains apply to crypto specifically.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The core rule: crypto is property, not currency

Since 2014, the IRS has treated cryptocurrency as property for federal tax purposes, the same broad category as stocks or real estate, not as foreign currency. This one classification decision, laid out in IRS Notice 2014-21, is the foundation for everything else in this guide.

Practically, this means that general tax principles for property sales, including capital gains and losses, apply to crypto, rather than the different rules that would apply if it were treated like currency.

What counts as a taxable event

A taxable event happens when you dispose of crypto, meaning you get rid of it in some way, or when you receive it as a form of income. Simply buying and holding is not, on its own, a taxable event.

QUICK REFERENCE
Action Taxable?
Buying crypto with US dollars and holding it No
Selling crypto for US dollars Yes
Trading one crypto for another Yes, see Is a Crypto-to-Crypto Trade Taxable?
Using crypto to buy goods or services Yes
Receiving crypto as payment for work Yes, as ordinary income
Mining or staking rewards Yes, as ordinary income when received
Receiving an airdrop or hard fork coins Yes, generally as ordinary income when received
Transferring crypto between your own wallets No, though you must still track cost basis correctly
Gifting crypto (within annual limits) Generally not taxable to the giver; different rules apply to the recipient later
Simplified. Specific situations can have nuances not captured in a quick table; confirm with a tax professional.

How capital gains work for crypto

When you dispose of crypto in a taxable way, you calculate a capital gain or loss: the difference between what you originally paid for it (your cost basis) and what you received when you disposed of it.

  • Short-term gain: from an asset held one year or less. Taxed as ordinary income, at your regular income tax rate, which can range from 10% to 37% depending on your total income.
  • Long-term gain: from an asset held more than one year. Taxed at preferential capital gains rates, generally 0%, 15%, or 20% depending on your income level.
Why the one-year mark matters so much

Holding an asset just past the one-year mark before selling can meaningfully change the tax rate that applies to any gain. This is a real, IRS-recognized distinction, not a loophole, and it's one of the few timing decisions actually within your control.

When crypto is taxed as ordinary income instead

Not all crypto tax follows the capital gains path. Crypto you receive as compensation or reward is generally taxed as ordinary income, based on its fair market value at the moment you received it:

  • Wages paid in crypto are reported similarly to regular wages.
  • Contractor payments received in crypto are generally reported as self-employment income.
  • Mining and staking rewards are taxed as ordinary income when received, based on their value at that time.
  • Airdrops and hard fork proceeds are generally treated the same way.

After that initial income event, if you later sell or trade the crypto you received, a separate capital gain or loss calculation applies to any change in value from the day you received it.

What changed with Form 1099-DA

Starting with the 2025 tax year, filed in 2026, centralized US exchanges are required to issue Form 1099-DA, reporting gross proceeds from digital asset sales directly to both you and the IRS. This is a significant change: the IRS now receives much of the same transaction data you do, closing a gap that previously relied heavily on individual self-reporting.

This reporting generally covers centralized exchanges. It generally does not cover self-custody wallet-to-wallet transfers, peer-to-peer transactions, or most decentralized finance (DeFi) activity, which remain your responsibility to track and report even without a form arriving in the mail.

Common mistake

Assuming that because no 1099 form arrived, nothing needs to be reported. The reporting requirement exists independently of whether you receive a form. This is covered in more depth in Do I Have to Report Crypto on My Taxes?

Why record-keeping matters more than ever

Current IRS guidance requires tracking cost basis on a per-wallet or per-account basis, rather than pooling everything together as one combined average, which was a method some taxpayers previously relied on. This makes accurate, organized records genuinely important, not just a good habit.

  • Keep records of the date, amount, and value at the time for every purchase, sale, trade, and crypto received as income.
  • Keep records separately for each wallet or account, rather than assuming they can all be blended together.
  • Consider dedicated crypto tax software, or a tax professional experienced with digital assets, especially if you've used multiple wallets or exchanges.

Keep in mind

  • Rules can change. Congress and the IRS continue to actively develop crypto tax guidance; always check irs.gov for the current rules before filing.
  • Penalties apply to underreporting, whether or not it was intentional, so accurate records matter.
  • This guide is general information, not a substitute for advice based on your specific tax situation.

articles.title: Two-Factor Authentication, Explained
articles.description: A five-minute setup that blocks the majority of account takeover attempts. Here's exactly how to turn it on.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What two-factor authentication is

Two-factor authentication (2FA, sometimes called multi-factor authentication) means proving who you are in two different ways to log in. The first is your password. The second is something else, like a code from an app on your phone or a physical key.

So even if someone steals or guesses your password, they still can't get in without the second factor.

Why it matters so much for crypto

  • Crypto moves fast and can't be reversed. One successful takeover can empty an account in minutes.
  • Stolen passwords are everywhere. Many people reuse passwords, and leaked databases are traded constantly.
  • Security agencies strongly recommend it. Researchers consistently find that 2FA blocks the large majority of automated account takeover attempts.
Set expectations

2FA is one of the best protections you can add for the least effort. It isn't perfect, but skipping it is one of the most common mistakes.

The main types, from good to best

COMPARISON
Method How it works Strength
Email code A code is sent to your email Weak. Only as safe as your email account
Text message (SMS) A code is texted to your phone Better than nothing, but can be defeated by SIM swapping
Authenticator app An app on your phone generates a changing code Strong for most people
Hardware security key or passkey A physical device or device-based credential you approve Strongest, and resistant to fake-site phishing
If a platform offers an authenticator app or a security key, choose one of those over text messages.

How to turn it on, step by step

Menus differ by platform, but the process is nearly always the same:

  1. Secure your email first. Email is the master key to your other accounts, so give it a strong, unique password and 2FA before anything else.
  2. Install an authenticator app from your phone's official app store, from a well-known provider.
  3. Open your exchange's security settings. Look for "Security," "2FA," or "Two-step verification."
  4. Choose "authenticator app." The site will show a QR code and a setup key.
  5. Scan the QR code with your authenticator app. It will start showing a 6-digit code that changes every 30 seconds or so.
  6. Type in the current code to confirm it works.
  7. Save your backup codes. Write them on paper and store them somewhere private. Do not screenshot them or save them in cloud notes.
  8. Turn on extra protections if offered, such as withdrawal address allow-lists, anti-phishing codes, or login alerts.
  9. Test it. Log out and log back in to be sure it works before you rely on it.

What is SIM swapping?

In a SIM swap, a criminal convinces your phone carrier to move your phone number to a SIM card they control. They then receive your text messages, including 2FA codes.

  • Prefer an authenticator app or security key over text messages.
  • Ask your carrier about adding an account PIN or a port-out lock.
  • Be careful about how much personal information is public online.

What if you lose your phone?

This is what backup codes are for. Without them, getting back into an account can be slow or impossible. Some authenticator apps also offer encrypted backups or easy transfer to a new phone. Check how yours works before you need it.

Common mistakes

  • Sharing a code with "support" or anyone who asks.
  • Approving login prompts you didn't trigger. Attackers sometimes spam prompts hoping you'll tap "approve" to make them stop.
  • Using the same password everywhere, which makes 2FA your only barrier.
  • Storing backup codes in a screenshot or an online note.
  • Relying on text-message 2FA when better options are available.

What 2FA doesn't do

  • It doesn't protect you from giving your details to a fake website in real time. See Fake Exchange Warning Signs.
  • It doesn't stop malware on a device that's already compromised.
  • It doesn't protect your recovery phrase. No app can, and you should never enter it anywhere online.

Keep in mind

  • Losing access to your 2FA without backups can lock you out.
  • No single measure is enough. Combine 2FA, unique passwords, and careful habits.
  • Settings change. Check each platform's current instructions.

articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.description: Most people who lose money to crypto scams aren't careless. They were reached at a bad moment by someone who was very good at their job.
articles.content:
Most people who lose money to crypto scams aren't careless. They were reached at a bad moment by someone who was very good at their job.

The scale is large. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) recorded more than 1,008,000 complaints and $20.877 billion in losses in 2025, a 26% jump from 2024. Investment scams were the costliest category at $8.65 billion, and about $7.2 billion of that involved cryptocurrency.

This guide is part of our Safety hub. It explains how these scams work, the warning signs to check, and what to do if you're already caught in one. New to crypto? Start with our Getting Started guide first.

The short version

  • Only scammers demand payment in crypto. No legitimate business or agency will require crypto for taxes, fines, or "protection" fees.
  • Crypto payments usually can't be undone. Unlike bank deposits, crypto isn't insured, and payments generally can't be reversed.
  • Urgency and secrecy are the biggest warning signs.
  • If you've been scammed: stop sending money, keep records, and report it. Never pay anyone who offers to get your money back.

Why crypto is a scammer's favorite tool

Sending crypto is fast, works across borders, and is hard to reverse. That combination makes stolen money easy to move and hard to recover.

Scammers also use AI. The FBI notes that investment scammers use it to generate thousands of conversations that each look different, so a message that feels personal may be one of thousands. To learn the terms used in this guide, such as wallet, seed phrase, and private key, see our crypto glossary.

The 5 most common crypto scams

Different stories, same goal: get you to send crypto, or hand over access to your wallet.

01

Romance-investment ("pig butchering")

A stranger builds trust online over weeks, often on dating or social apps, then introduces a "can't-lose" crypto opportunity. The FTC's rule: never mix online dating and investment advice.

02

Fake trading platforms

A slick site or app shows growing profits, but your deposit goes straight to scammers. When you try to withdraw, new "fees" or "taxes" appear first.

03

Impersonators and fake giveaways

Fake celebrities promise to multiply whatever you send. Others pose as government agencies, your bank, or tech support.

04

Crypto ATM scams

Most ATM losses start with government, business, or tech-support impersonation, and people over 60 are hit hardest. Some scammers stay on the phone and walk victims through the machine.

05

Phishing and wallet theft

Fake support agents, fake wallet apps, and look-alike sites ask for your seed phrase. Anyone who has it can empty your wallet.

8 red flags to check before you send anything

If even one of these shows up, stop and get a second opinion.

01

Guaranteed or unusually high returns

Real investments carry risk, and honest people say so.

02

Pressure to act right now

"Limited spots" and "your account will be closed" are built to stop you from thinking.

03

A stranger online gives investment advice

Someone you've only met online has no reason to manage your money.

04

You must pay in crypto, gift cards, or by ATM

These are hard to trace and hard to reverse, which is exactly why scammers ask.

05

You're told to keep it secret

Being told not to talk to family, bank staff, or store employees is a major red flag.

06

You're told exactly which machine or wallet to use

Being sent to a specific crypto ATM, and urged to go immediately, is a scripted-scam sign.

07

You see profits but can't withdraw

A new fee appears every time you try.

08

Anyone asks for your seed phrase

Legitimate companies never do. Never share it, with anyone, for any reason.

5 quick checks before you invest

  • ✓Search the company name plus "scam" and "complaints."
  • ✓Confirm the platform is registered and regulated in the US. Our exchanges guide explains what to look for.
  • ✓Type the web address yourself instead of clicking links in messages.
  • ✓Test with a tiny amount and try withdrawing it before adding more.
  • ✓Tell someone you trust before sending money. A five-minute pause blocks many scams.

Worried about keeping your own crypto safe? See how wallets and custody work before you buy anything.

If you've been scammed: step by step

You are not alone, and it is not your fault. Take these steps in order.

01

Stop sending money

Don't pay any "release" or "withdrawal" fee. The FBI's first instruction to victims is to stop sending money to the scammers.
02

Save the evidence

Screenshots of chats, web addresses, phone numbers, usernames. Most important: wallet addresses, amounts and type of crypto, transaction hashes, and dates and times.
03

Report to the FBI

File at ic3.gov, or contact your local FBI field office, with as much transaction information as you have. Report even if you're missing details.
04

Report to the FTC and alert your exchange

File at reportfraud.ftc.gov. If the scam involved buying, selling, or moving crypto, you can also report to the SEC and CFTC, and tell the exchange you used.
05

Contact your bank and police

Call your bank or card company right away if money left through them, and file a local police report. Some banks ask for a report number. Scam losses can also affect your taxes, so see our taxes guide and ask a tax professional.
06

Secure your accounts

Change passwords, turn on two-factor authentication, and move funds out of any wallet whose seed phrase you shared.

Beware of "recovery" services

After a scam, many victims are contacted again by companies promising to get the money back. This is a second scam. The FBI logged more than 10,500 recovery-scam complaints in 2025, with an estimated $1.4 billion in losses.

Private recovery companies can't issue seizure orders, and exchanges freeze accounts only through internal processes or legal process. IC3 never contacts you for money and doesn't work with law firms or crypto services to recover funds. Be suspicious of anyone who reaches out first, promises results, or wants payment before doing any work.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get my crypto back after a scam?

Sometimes, but it's difficult and never guaranteed. Reporting quickly with full transaction details gives law enforcement the best chance. The FBI's Operation Level Up, which alerts victims of ongoing crypto investment scams, has reduced potential losses by more than $500 million since 2024.

Are crypto ATMs safe?

The machines aren't the problem, but they're a favorite tool for scammers. If anyone tells you to use one to protect your money or fix a problem, it's a scam.

Is it my fault if I was scammed?

No. These are organized operations built to fool intelligent people. Reporting helps investigators stop the next victim.

Do legitimate exchanges ever ask for my seed phrase?

Never.

Bottom line: crypto scams work by making you feel rushed, special, and alone. Slow down, verify, and tell someone. If something feels off, it probably is.

Think you've been targeted?

Tell us what happened. We can't recover funds or give personal financial advice, and we will never ask you for money or your seed phrase.

Is It Too Late to Invest in Crypto?
articles.description: A fair, non-hyped answer to one of the most common beginner questions, including why “timing” isn't the only thing that matters.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The short, honest answer

Nobody can tell you whether it's "too late," and anyone who says they can is guessing or selling something.

What we can do is explain why the question is harder than it looks, and offer better questions to ask instead. The right answer for one person can be very different from the right answer for another, because it depends on your goals, your finances, and how much risk you can genuinely handle.

Why so many people ask this

Most beginners hear crypto stories the same way: someone bought early and did extremely well. Those stories are memorable and get shared widely, which makes it feel like the opportunity has already passed.

That feeling has a name, FOMO (fear of missing out), and it's one of the biggest drivers of poor financial decisions. It pushes people to buy quickly, at emotional moments, often near peaks of excitement.

Worth knowing

The stories you hear are a filtered sample. Thousands of cryptocurrencies have faded away or gone to near zero, but those stories rarely get retold. This is called survivorship bias, and it makes the winners look more common than they are.

What "late" would even mean

When people say "late," they usually mean "the biggest price gains are behind us." But that's a prediction, and nobody can honestly make it in either direction.

  • Bitcoin's earliest years came with risks most people today wouldn't accept: tiny markets, no regulation, exchanges failing, and no certainty it would survive at all.
  • Today's market is different. It is larger, more regulated, and more widely known, which changes both the opportunity and the risks. It does not make outcomes more predictable.
  • A high price isn't proof of anything. A price can be high or low without telling you whether the next move is up or down.

What history shows, and what it doesn't

Crypto prices have gone through repeated cycles of rapid rises followed by steep falls. Drops of more than half from a peak have happened several times in Bitcoin's history, and many smaller cryptocurrencies have fallen much further.

It's fair to point that out. It's not fair to treat it as a forecast. Past performance doesn't predict future results, whether that past looks wonderful or terrible.

A useful way to think about it

History can teach you how volatile crypto has been. It can't tell you what happens next. Plan for the volatility, not for a particular outcome.

Why timing isn't the only thing that matters

People spend enormous energy trying to pick the perfect moment. But for most individuals, these factors have a bigger effect on how things turn out:

  • How much you put in. Investing money you can't afford to lose is a bigger risk than picking a slightly wrong day.
  • How you react to drops. Panic-selling after a fall, or buying more out of excitement after a rise, often hurts more than the entry point itself.
  • Security. Losing funds to a scam or a lost recovery phrase is a far more common way to end up with nothing than "bad timing."
  • Fees and taxes. Trading frequently can add costs and tax paperwork that quietly reduce results.
  • What it is. "Crypto" covers very different assets. Timing matters little if you don't understand what you're buying.

Better questions to ask than "am I too late?"

  1. Do I understand what I'd be buying and how it works?
  2. Could I lose all of this money without it changing my life?
  3. How would I feel, and what would I do, if it dropped by half next month?
  4. Do I have an emergency fund and manageable debt already?
  5. Am I making this decision calmly, or because I feel rushed?

If you can't answer those comfortably, waiting and learning is a perfectly reasonable choice. Not investing is also a choice, and nothing is wrong with making it.

If you're still curious

  • Keep learning first. Read the rest of the Getting Started guides before any money moves.
  • If you decide to try, consider a small amount you can afford to lose. See How Much Money Do You Need to Start?
  • Consider spreading purchases over time rather than one large buy. See Dollar-Cost Averaging.
  • Talk to a licensed financial advisor if this is a meaningful part of your savings.

Risks to understand

  • Volatility: large swings in either direction can happen quickly.
  • Total loss is possible: some crypto assets have gone to near zero and never recovered.
  • No insurance: crypto holdings generally lack the protections of bank deposits.
  • Emotional decisions: FOMO and panic are the most common causes of avoidable losses.
  • Scams: urgency and "last chance" messaging are common warning signs.

articles.title: Is a Crypto-to-Crypto Trade Taxable?
articles.description: A commonly misunderstood rule: yes, trading one coin for another can trigger taxes, even if you never touched US dollars.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The direct answer

Yes. Trading one cryptocurrency for another, for example swapping Ethereum for a different token, is a taxable event under current IRS guidance. This holds true even though no US dollars were involved anywhere in the transaction.

Why this surprises so many people

It's an intuitive but incorrect assumption that taxes only apply when you convert crypto "back into real money." Because crypto is classified as property, not currency, the same rule that applies to trading one stock for another, without ever touching cash in between, also applies here.

The way the IRS actually sees it

A crypto-to-crypto trade is treated as two things happening simultaneously: you sold your first asset at its current dollar value, and separately used those proceeds to buy the second asset. The "sale" half of that is what creates the taxable event.

How the gain or loss is actually calculated

For a trade of Coin A for Coin B:

  1. Determine the fair market value of Coin A, in US dollars, at the exact time of the trade.
  2. Subtract your original cost basis in Coin A from that value. This is your capital gain or loss on Coin A.
  3. Your cost basis in the newly acquired Coin B becomes that same fair market value figure, which matters for calculating gain or loss whenever you eventually dispose of Coin B.

So a single crypto-to-crypto trade actually creates a taxable event now (on the coin you gave up) and sets a new starting point for tax purposes on the coin you received.

A simplified, hypothetical example

Suppose you originally bought 1 unit of Coin A for $1,000. Later, when Coin A is worth $4,000, you trade all of it for units of Coin B. No dollars changed hands at any point.

HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE — ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY
Step Amount
Original cost basis in Coin A $1,000
Value of Coin A at the time of the trade $4,000
Taxable capital gain on Coin A $3,000
New cost basis in Coin B received $4,000
These numbers are made up purely to show the mechanics, not a prediction or real transaction data.

That $3,000 gain is taxable in the year the trade happened, regardless of whether Coin B is later sold, held, or itself later loses value.

Situations where this rule commonly applies

  • Swapping tokens on a decentralized exchange (DEX).
  • Converting one coin to a stablecoin, which is still a crypto-to-crypto trade, even though a stablecoin is designed to track the dollar. See What Is a Stablecoin?
  • Trading within an exchange's interface without withdrawing to a bank account at any point.
  • Some DeFi transactions, such as certain liquidity pool deposits or withdrawals, which can also involve token exchanges. These can be more complex; consult a tax professional for specifics.
Common mistake

Thinking that converting volatile crypto into a stablecoin "doesn't count" because a stablecoin isn't as exciting or volatile as other tokens. Tax-wise, it's treated the same as any other crypto-to-crypto trade.

Why this makes tracking so important

Frequent trading between different cryptocurrencies can generate a large number of individual taxable events within a single year, each needing its own fair market value calculation at the time of the trade. This is one of the strongest practical arguments for using dedicated crypto tax software rather than trying to reconstruct values manually later.

Keep in mind

  • Every crypto-to-crypto trade needs to be tracked and reported, not just conversions to dollars.
  • Fair market value at the exact time of the trade is what matters, which can require careful record-keeping for frequent traders.
  • This is one of the most commonly missed reporting obligations among newer crypto users.
EDUCATIONAL CONTENT — NOT TAX ADVICE

This article is general educational information, not personalized tax advice. Tax situations vary by individual, and tax rules can change. Consult a licensed tax professional or CPA about your specific circumstances, and verify current rules directly on irs.gov before filing.

articles.title: Market Cap
articles.description: The total value of all coins of a given cryptocurrency in circulation — one basic way (not the only way) people compare the size of different coins.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

Market cap, short for market capitalization, is the total value of every coin of a specific cryptocurrency currently in circulation. It's calculated as:

The formula

Market cap = current price per coin × total number of coins in circulation

Why people use it

Market cap gives a rough sense of a cryptocurrency's overall size, which is often more meaningful than looking at the price of a single coin in isolation. It's commonly used to broadly group cryptocurrencies into categories like "large-cap," "mid-cap," and "small-cap," similar to how these terms are used for stocks.

The pricing mistake it helps avoid

A cryptocurrency priced at $0.01 isn't automatically "cheaper" or a better deal than one priced at $50,000. What matters is how many total coins exist. A coin priced at a fraction of a cent, but with trillions of coins in circulation, can have a larger total market cap than a coin priced much higher with a small supply.

Common mistake

Assuming a coin with a very low per-coin price has "more room to grow" than an expensive one. Price per coin depends entirely on how the total supply happens to be divided, and tells you nothing on its own about the project's size or potential. This exact confusion is covered further in What Is an Altcoin?

What market cap doesn't tell you

  • It doesn't reflect how easy an asset is to actually buy or sell at that value. See Slippage.
  • It can be distorted if a large share of coins is held by a small number of wallets and rarely traded.
  • A high market cap doesn't mean low risk. Even large-cap cryptocurrencies remain volatile and speculative.
  • It says nothing about the project's actual product, team, or use case on its own.

Keep in mind

  • Market cap is one data point, not a complete evaluation. Use it alongside the other factors covered in What Is an Altcoin?
  • Reported figures can vary slightly between different data sources, depending on how "circulating supply" is defined for a specific coin.

articles.title: Crypto Wallets for Beginners
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.description: Before you buy anything, you need somewhere to keep it. This guide walks through what a wallet is and the basic types, in plain language.
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What a crypto wallet actually is

Despite the name, a crypto wallet doesn't hold coins the way a leather wallet holds cash. Your coins always live on the blockchain, the shared record we explained in How Does Cryptocurrency Actually Work?

What a wallet holds is your keys: the secret information that proves you're allowed to move the coins that belong to your address. A better comparison is a keyring, not a purse. Whoever holds the keys controls the coins.

The one idea to remember

A wallet doesn't store your crypto. It stores the keys that prove it's yours. That's why protecting the keys matters more than anything else in this guide.

Public address, private key, and recovery phrase

Three pieces show up in almost every wallet:

  • Public address: like an account number. You share it so others can send you crypto. Sharing it is safe.
  • Private key: the secret that authorizes spending. Never share it.
  • Recovery phrase (or seed phrase): a list of usually 12 or 24 words that can rebuild your wallet and all its private keys on a new device. It's your master backup.

The recovery phrase is the most important item you'll ever handle in crypto. Anyone who has it can take everything in the wallet, and if you lose it and your device breaks, there is normally no way to get your funds back. There is no "forgot password" button.

The main types of wallets

Wallets are usually grouped by two questions: who holds the keys, and whether the wallet is connected to the internet.

COMPARISON
Type Who holds the keys Convenience Main risk
Exchange account The exchange (custodial) Very easy, feels like a normal app Depends on the company's security and solvency; you can be locked out
Software wallet (mobile, desktop, browser) You (non-custodial) Easy; always online ("hot") Malware, phishing, fake apps, lost phone
Hardware wallet You (non-custodial) Less convenient; keys stay on a small offline device ("cold") Losing the device or phrase; buying a tampered or fake device
Simplified. Each type has trade-offs, and none is automatically "safe."

Custodial means a company holds the keys for you, much like a bank holds your money. Non-custodial means you hold them yourself, which gives you full control and full responsibility. A common saying in crypto is "not your keys, not your coins," which is a short way of describing that trade-off.

Hot wallets are connected to the internet, which makes them convenient and more exposed to online attacks. Cold wallets keep keys offline, which makes remote theft much harder but adds some hassle.

How to choose what fits you

There's no single best wallet, only a better fit for your situation. Some honest questions to ask yourself:

  • How much am I holding? Small amounts you're still learning with are a different situation from a larger sum you plan to keep for years.
  • Am I comfortable being my own bank? Self-custody means no one can help if you lose your phrase.
  • How often will I move it? Frequent activity favors convenience; long-term holding can favor offline storage.
  • Is this wallet from a reputable, well-reviewed source? Look for an established track record, not just a slick website.

Many beginners start with a reputable exchange account while they learn, and consider moving to their own wallet as the amount or their confidence grows. That's a reasonable path to consider, not a rule.

Setting up a wallet safely

  1. Get the app or device from the official source only. Go to the maker's real website by typing it yourself, not by clicking an ad or search result.
  2. Write your recovery phrase on paper, by hand. Store it somewhere private and protected from fire and water.
  3. Never store the phrase digitally. No screenshots, no notes app, no email, no cloud storage.
  4. Check the phrase once. Confirm you wrote every word correctly and in order.
  5. Turn on every security option. Set a strong PIN or password, and enable two-factor authentication on any exchange account.
  6. Do a small test first. Send a tiny amount, confirm it arrives, and only then move more.

Common and costly mistakes

Common mistake

Typing your recovery phrase into a website or app to "fix" or "verify" your wallet. This is one of the most common ways people lose everything. Legitimate wallets never ask you to enter your phrase online.

  • Fake wallet apps and lookalike websites that copy the real thing.
  • Buying a hardware wallet from a third-party reseller or marketplace, where it may have been tampered with. Buy directly from the manufacturer.
  • Sending on the wrong network. Some coins exist on several networks, and sending to an address on a different network can mean permanent loss. Double-check network and address every time.
  • Copying an address by hand. Copy and paste, then verify the first and last few characters. Some malware swaps addresses in your clipboard.
  • "Support" strangers who message you first offering help. Real support does not cold-contact you or ask for your phrase.

Risks to understand

  • You are the security team. With self-custody, mistakes are usually unfixable.
  • Lost phrase, lost funds. There's typically no recovery route.
  • Exchange risk. Funds on a platform depend on that company's security and financial health, and crypto holdings aren't insured like bank deposits.
  • Device and software risk. Phones get lost, software has bugs, and attackers target wallets specifically.
  • Price risk. Whatever the storage method, the value of what you hold can fall sharply.

articles.title: HODL
articles.description: Crypto slang for holding onto an asset long-term instead of selling during price swings. Originally a misspelling of “hold” that stuck.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

HODL means holding onto a cryptocurrency for the long term, rather than selling during short-term price swings. It's used as a noun, a verb, and often shouted in all capital letters as encouragement during a market downturn: "just HODL."

Where the word came from

The term traces back to a 2013 post on a Bitcoin discussion forum, titled "I AM HODLING," in which the author, apparently while stressed and possibly having had a drink, misspelled "holding." The typo was embraced by the community and has stuck ever since.

Over time, people have also jokingly reinterpreted it as a backronym for "Hold On for Dear Life," which captures the emotional tone it's often used with, even though that's not how the term actually originated.

How it's used today

"HODLing" generally describes a passive, long-term approach: buying crypto and resisting the urge to sell based on short-term price movements, whether the market is dropping sharply or rising quickly.

The idea behind it

The term captures a real, well-documented behavioral pattern: many investors sell out of panic during a downturn, and buy out of excitement during a rally, both of which can hurt long-term results. "HODL" is shorthand for resisting both impulses.

Where the term can be misused

"HODL" can be used constructively as a reminder about emotional discipline, but it can also be used to talk someone out of a reasonable decision to sell, especially by people promoting a specific coin who benefit from others continuing to hold it.

Common mistake

Treating "HODL" as a reason to ignore your own risk tolerance or financial situation. Holding through volatility only makes sense if you could genuinely afford the position going to zero in the first place. See How Much Money Do You Need to Start?

Risks to understand

  • "Just HODL" isn't advice tailored to you. Your actual circumstances, timeline, and risk tolerance matter more than a slogan.
  • Holding doesn't guarantee recovery. Some assets that people held through a downturn never returned to their previous value.
  • Community pressure can discourage a reasonable sale. A decision to sell can be perfectly sound even if it goes against the loudest voices in a community.

articles.title: Cold Wallet
articles.description: A wallet that stores your crypto offline, disconnected from the internet, making it much harder to hack remotely.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

A cold wallet is a way of storing crypto private keys completely offline, never connected to the internet during normal use. This is the opposite of a hot wallet, which stays connected to the internet for convenience. The most common form of cold wallet is a dedicated hardware device, covered in full in Hardware Wallet vs. Software Wallet.

Why offline storage matters

Most theft of crypto happens remotely: through phishing, malware, or fake apps that trick an internet-connected device into revealing keys or approving a malicious transaction. A cold wallet's keys are never exposed to an internet-connected device during the parts of the process that matter most, which removes most of that attack surface entirely.

A simple analogy

A hot wallet is like cash in your pocket while you're out and about; convenient, but exposed to pickpockets. A cold wallet is like cash locked in a safe at home; less convenient to access, but far harder for someone to remotely reach.

The main forms a cold wallet takes

  • Hardware wallets: small dedicated devices built specifically for this purpose, the most common and generally recommended cold storage method for most people.
  • Paper wallets: keys or a seed phrase written or printed on physical paper. This older method is less commonly recommended today, since paper can degrade, burn, or be lost with no digital backup at all.
  • Air-gapped devices: a computer or device that has never been, and never will be, connected to the internet, used exclusively for signing transactions offline. This is a more advanced setup, generally used by people holding significant amounts.

The trade-off compared to a hot wallet

Cold storage meaningfully reduces exposure to remote hacking, but it adds friction: you need the physical device or item on hand to approve a transaction, which makes cold wallets better suited to holdings you don't need to access frequently, rather than funds used for everyday transactions.

Common mistake

Assuming "cold" automatically means "safe no matter what." A cold wallet still depends entirely on how well you protect the device itself and its backup phrase. Losing both means losing access just as permanently as any other method.

Risks to understand

  • Physical loss, damage, or theft of the device or paper remains a real risk.
  • The backup recovery phrase is still the ultimate safety net, and protecting it matters just as much as the device itself.
  • Buying a device from an untrusted reseller can undermine the security benefits entirely, as covered in Hardware Wallet vs. Software Wallet.

articles.title: Is Coinbase Regulated?
articles.description: A factual answer to a commonly searched question — explained clearly, without this being an endorsement of any specific platform.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

Why this question comes up so often

"Is Coinbase regulated?" is one of the most commonly searched questions about crypto exchanges, largely because Coinbase is one of the most widely used platforms in the US. This guide answers it factually, as of September 2026. Regulatory status can change, so always verify current details directly with the regulators listed below or the company's own disclosures before relying on this.

The short answer

Yes, in several specific and verifiable ways, though the picture is more layered than a simple yes or no. Coinbase operates under multiple overlapping forms of US regulation, but it is not registered with the SEC as a securities exchange or broker-dealer for its core crypto trading platform.

Both of those things are true at once, and understanding why requires looking at the different pieces separately.

It's a public, SEC-reporting company

Coinbase Global, Inc. is a publicly traded company listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker COIN. As a public company, it's required to file regular reports, including quarterly 10-Q and annual 10-K filings, with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which are publicly available on the SEC's EDGAR database.

This means Coinbase's business as a company is subject to SEC reporting and disclosure rules. It does not mean that every crypto asset traded on its platform is registered with the SEC as a security, or that the trading platform itself is registered as a securities exchange.

It's a registered money services business

Coinbase is registered with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) as a money services business, which subjects it to federal anti-money laundering and Bank Secrecy Act requirements. It also holds money transmitter licenses in states across the US, and separately holds a New York State "BitLicense" for virtual currency business activity, issued by the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS).

A newer development: a national trust bank charter

In April 2026, Coinbase received conditional approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) to operate a subsidiary, Coinbase National Trust Company, as a federally chartered trust bank. Conditional approval is a preliminary step; the company still needs to satisfy specific conditions before that charter becomes fully operational.

If completed, this would place that part of Coinbase's business under direct federal banking oversight from the OCC, rather than relying solely on the current state-by-state money transmitter licensing structure.

What it is not registered as

Coinbase's own SEC filings have stated plainly that its core trading platform is not registered or licensed with the SEC as a national securities exchange, broker-dealer, or alternative trading system (ATS). This is an important distinction: being a publicly traded, SEC-reporting company is different from the trading platform itself being registered under securities exchange rules.

The SEC has also brought enforcement actions against Coinbase in the past regarding whether certain assets offered on its platform should have been registered as securities. Search the SEC's own litigation releases for the current status of any such matters, since legal proceedings evolve over time.

Summary

AS OF SEPTEMBER 2026 — VERIFY CURRENT STATUS DIRECTLY
Regulatory status Yes / No / Nuanced
Publicly traded, SEC-reporting company Yes
Registered as a money services business (FinCEN) Yes
Licensed as a money transmitter in most states Yes
Holds a NYDFS BitLicense Yes
Conditional approval for an OCC national trust bank charter Yes, conditional, as of April 2026
Registered with the SEC as a securities exchange or broker-dealer No, per the company's own SEC filings

How you can verify this yourself

  • Search Coinbase Global, Inc. directly on the SEC's EDGAR database (sec.gov/edgar) for its public filings.
  • Check NYDFS's public licensing records for its BitLicense status.
  • Check the OCC's public announcements for updates on the national trust bank charter.
  • For any other platform, run the same kind of check yourself using Is This Exchange Legit?, rather than relying on marketing claims.

Keep in mind

  • "Regulated" doesn't mean risk-free. Even heavily regulated platforms carry the general risks of crypto covered throughout this site, including price volatility.
  • Regulatory status changes over time. New approvals, licenses, or enforcement actions can shift this picture.
  • This guide is not a recommendation to use Coinbase or any other specific platform. We don't endorse or rank exchanges.
