articles.title: What Is a Stablecoin?
articles.description: Coins designed to hold a steady value — and the specific risks that come with that design, including what happens if the “peg” breaks.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What a stablecoin is

Most cryptocurrencies can swing sharply in price within a single day. A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency specifically designed to avoid that, by keeping its value tied, or "pegged," to something steady, almost always the US dollar.

In practice, one unit of a dollar-pegged stablecoin is meant to always be worth about one dollar. That stability is what makes stablecoins useful as a way to hold or move money within crypto without constantly worrying about price swings.

Why people use them

  • A resting place between trades. Selling a volatile coin into a stablecoin lets someone step back from price swings without fully leaving crypto.
  • Moving money quickly. Stablecoins can move across borders faster than some traditional transfers.
  • Access to dollars where they're scarce. In some countries with unstable local currencies or capital controls, stablecoins are used as an accessible substitute for dollars.
  • Use inside decentralized finance (DeFi). Many DeFi activities are priced and settled in stablecoins. See What Is DeFi in Crypto?

The three main types

COMPARISON
Type How it holds its value Example approach
Fiat-backed Reserves of real dollars and short-term assets held by a company, ideally redeemable 1-for-1 Most large stablecoins work this way
Crypto-backed Other cryptocurrencies locked up as collateral, usually worth more than the stablecoins issued, to absorb price swings Used by some decentralized projects
Algorithmic Computer code and market incentives try to hold the price steady, without full asset backing Considered the riskiest category

Fiat-backed is currently the most common and widely used approach. It's worth knowing that not all fiat-backed issuers disclose their reserves the same way; independent audits and clear reporting vary between companies.

How a peg is supposed to work

For a fiat-backed stablecoin, the idea is straightforward: for every coin in circulation, the issuer holds a dollar (or dollar-equivalent asset) in reserve, and will exchange coins for real dollars on request. That redemption promise is what's supposed to keep the market price near one dollar.

Crypto-backed and algorithmic designs try to achieve the same steady price using different mechanisms, generally without one company holding matching dollar reserves.

What happens when a peg breaks

A stablecoin "depegging" means its market price moves noticeably away from its target, even briefly. This has actually happened:

  • TerraUSD (UST), May 2022. An algorithmic stablecoin that was not backed by real dollar reserves lost its peg and collapsed to near zero within days, wiping out tens of billions of dollars and setting off a wider crypto market downturn.
  • USD Coin (USDC), March 2023. A portion of USDC's cash reserves were held at Silicon Valley Bank when it failed. USDC briefly traded as low as around $0.87 before recovering to near $1.00 once reserve access was confirmed.
Why this matters

These two examples show very different outcomes. An algorithmic design with no real backing collapsed permanently. A fiat-backed coin recovered once its reserves were confirmed safe. The design behind a stablecoin materially changes the risk, which is exactly why it's worth understanding before you rely on one.

Risks to understand

  • Reserve risk. A fiat-backed stablecoin is only as strong as the assets actually backing it and how transparently that's reported.
  • Algorithmic risk. Designs without real asset backing have failed completely before and could again.
  • No deposit insurance. Stablecoins are not covered by FDIC insurance, even though they're pegged to the dollar.
  • Redemption isn't guaranteed instantly. During stress, redemptions can be paused or delayed.
  • Regulatory change. Rules for stablecoin issuers are still developing in the US and could affect how they operate.
  • "Stable" isn't "risk-free." It only addresses one kind of risk, price volatility, not the others listed here.

articles.title: Blockchain
articles.description: A shared, public record of transactions that many computers agree on together, instead of one central authority keeping the books.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

A blockchain is a shared record of transactions, kept in matching copies by many separate computers instead of one central company or authority. New transactions are grouped into blocks, and each block links to the one before it, forming a chain that runs back to the very first entry.

Why it's built that way

The design exists to answer one question: can a group of people who don't necessarily trust each other still agree on a shared, honest record, without a bank or government in the middle? Having thousands of independent copies, all checking each other, is how a blockchain achieves that.

The picture to keep in mind

A blockchain is like a shared notebook that thousands of people keep an identical copy of. Nobody owns the notebook, and a fake entry in one copy simply won't match everyone else's.

What it's actually used for

Cryptocurrencies are the most well-known use of blockchain technology, but the idea has also been explored for other kinds of record-keeping, including supply chain tracking and some government and financial pilot projects. Owning a cryptocurrency means having an entry on its blockchain that says a certain address controls a certain amount.

Why the word gets used as marketing

Because "blockchain" sounds technical and trustworthy, it's often used in marketing for products that may not actually need one, or that don't work the way they claim to.

Common mistake

Assuming that because something "uses blockchain," it must be secure, innovative, or a good investment. The technology only guarantees that the record is hard to alter after the fact. It says nothing about whether the project behind it is honest or worthwhile. See How to Spot a Crypto Scam.

articles.title: What Is Bitcoin, Really?
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.description: A plain-language explanation of what Bitcoin is, how new coins are created, and why people compare it to digital gold — without the jargon
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What Bitcoin actually is

Bitcoin is a digital currency that exists only as entries on a shared, public ledger called a blockchain. No bank or company controls it. Instead, a global network of computers verifies every transaction and agrees on the record together.

Because that ledger is public and extremely hard to alter after the fact, Bitcoin can move value between two people anywhere in the world without a bank in the middle. That's the core idea most other explanations bury under jargon.

Each unit of Bitcoin can be divided into much smaller pieces — the smallest is called a "satoshi," named after Bitcoin's creator. You don't need to buy a whole Bitcoin to own some; most people buy small fractions of one.

Common mistake

Treating "Bitcoin" and "crypto" as interchangeable. Bitcoin is one specific asset with its own rules — thousands of other cryptocurrencies work very differently and carry very different risks.

A brief history

Bitcoin was introduced in 2008 through a document called a whitepaper, published under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto — the real identity behind that name has never been confirmed. The network itself went live in January 2009.

The idea was to create money that didn't depend on a bank or government to function, especially in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, when trust in traditional financial institutions had taken a hit. Since then, Bitcoin has gone through many cycles of rapid price increases followed by steep declines — a pattern worth understanding before you consider it, covered more in the risks section below.

How new bitcoins are created

New bitcoins are released through a process called mining. Computers around the world compete to solve a complex mathematical puzzle, and whoever solves it first gets to add the next "block" of transactions to the chain — and receives newly created bitcoin as a reward.

This process is deliberately designed to require real computing power and electricity, which is what makes the network secure: altering past records would require redoing an enormous amount of that work all over again.

  • Total supply is capped at 21 million bitcoins. No more will ever be created, by design.
  • The mining reward gets cut in half roughly every four years, an event called "the halving." This is one reason people point to Bitcoin's fixed scarcity.
  • Most people never mine. They simply buy existing bitcoin through an exchange, which is a separate process from mining entirely.
In plain terms

Mining is how new coins enter circulation and how the network stays secure — it is not something the average beginner needs to do, or should try to do casually. Home mining is generally not profitable once electricity costs are factored in.

How a Bitcoin transaction works

Say you want to send someone bitcoin. Here's the simplified version of what happens:

  1. You create a transaction using your wallet, specifying the recipient's address and the amount.
  2. You confirm it using your private key — proof that you actually own the funds you're sending.
  3. The transaction is broadcast to the network, where computers check that you actually have the funds and haven't already spent them elsewhere.
  4. Once verified, it's bundled into a block and added to the blockchain — at that point, it's considered confirmed and generally can't be reversed.

That last point matters: unlike a bank transfer, there's usually no "undo" button. This is exactly why understanding what you're doing before you send anything is so important.

Why it's called "digital gold"

People compare Bitcoin to gold for a few specific reasons, not just as a marketing phrase:

  • Scarcity — like gold, there's a hard limit on how much can ever exist.
  • No central issuer — no government can simply create more of it the way currencies can be printed.
  • Store-of-value narrative — some investors treat it as a long-term hedge, similar to how gold is sometimes used, though this comparison is debated and unproven over the long run.
  • Portability and divisibility — unlike physical gold, it can be sent anywhere in the world in minutes and divided into tiny fractions.

This comparison explains the reasoning some investors use — it is not a guarantee that Bitcoin will behave like gold, hold its value like gold, or protect against inflation the way people sometimes claim gold does.

Common misconceptions

  • "Bitcoin is anonymous." It's actually pseudonymous — every transaction is publicly visible on the blockchain forever, just not directly tied to your name unless that link is made elsewhere.
  • "Bitcoin has no real value because it's not backed by anything." This is a genuine debate among economists — but the same could be said of most modern currencies, which also aren't backed by physical assets like gold anymore.
  • "You have to buy a whole Bitcoin." You can buy any fraction of one, down to very small amounts.
  • "Bitcoin transactions are instant and free." Confirmation can take minutes, and network fees vary depending on demand.

Risks to understand

This isn't optional reading. Before you consider Bitcoin, understand that:

  • Price volatility is extreme. Double-digit percentage swings in a single day are not unusual.
  • There's no government insurance on Bitcoin holdings, unlike bank deposits.
  • Transactions are irreversible. A mistaken transfer or a successful scam generally cannot be undone.
  • Losing your private key or seed phrase means losing access permanently — there's no "forgot password" option.
  • Regulation is still evolving in the US and globally, which can affect taxes, access, and legality over time.

None of this means Bitcoin is inherently good or bad — it means it carries real, specific risks that are different from traditional assets, and you should understand them fully before deciding anything.

articles.title: Memecoin Risk, Explained
articles.description: Why coins based on internet jokes carry a specific and often extreme kind of risk that's worth understanding before you consider one.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What a memecoin is

A memecoin is a cryptocurrency created around an internet joke, meme, or cultural trend, rather than a specific technical purpose or product. Some have gained large followings and significant trading volume, purely from attention and community enthusiasm.

The defining feature of a memecoin isn't its blockchain or technology. It's that its main draw is humor, community, or viral attention, often with little or no separate stated purpose.

Why they carry a specific kind of risk

Most assets, even risky ones, have some argument for underlying value: a network effect, a working product, or a scarce, capped supply. A memecoin's value is driven almost entirely by attention and sentiment, which can shift extremely quickly and for reasons that have nothing to do with any underlying substance.

The core issue

When a coin's value is based mainly on how much attention it's getting, that value can disappear as fast as the attention does, with essentially nothing underneath to slow the fall.

Common patterns worth recognizing

  • Extreme, rapid price swings, often far larger and faster than more established cryptocurrencies.
  • Concentrated ownership. A small number of wallets, sometimes including the creators, often hold a very large share of the total supply.
  • Pump-and-dump patterns. Coordinated buying and promotion drives the price up quickly, early or large holders sell into that excitement, and the price then collapses, often leaving later buyers with steep losses.
  • Influencer promotion, sometimes paid and undisclosed, that can create a false sense of legitimacy or broad support.
  • Short attention lifespan. Many memecoins see intense interest for days or weeks, then fade into obscurity as attention moves elsewhere.
  • Overlap with rug pulls. The low barrier to creating a memecoin makes this category a common vehicle for the collapse pattern described in Crypto Rug Pull, Meaning.

How this differs from investing in Bitcoin or Ethereum

Bitcoin and Ethereum are also volatile and speculative, as covered elsewhere in this hub, but each has years of continuous development, real usage, and a stated purpose behind it that goes beyond attention alone.

Memecoins generally don't have that same foundation. That doesn't automatically make every memecoin a scam, some are created and traded with full awareness that they're speculative and community-driven, but it does mean the risk profile is fundamentally different and, on the whole, considerably higher.

Honest questions to ask before considering one

  1. Am I only interested because I'm afraid of missing out on a viral trend?
  2. Do I understand who created this and how much of the supply they control?
  3. Could I genuinely afford to lose this entire amount without it affecting my life?
  4. Am I being pushed toward buying quickly by hype, a countdown, or a promoter?
  5. If the attention around this disappeared tomorrow, what would be left?

If you decide to engage with one anyway

  • Treat any amount you put in as money you have fully accepted you may lose completely.
  • Be skeptical of ownership concentration and unverified claims about "locked" supply or team allocations.
  • Don't let a low price per coin create a false sense of it being "cheap." See the pricing misconception covered in What Is an Altcoin?
  • Recognize that timing an exit from a purely attention-driven asset is exceptionally difficult, even for experienced traders.

Risks to understand

  • Total loss is common, not a rare edge case, for this category specifically.
  • Extreme volatility, often more severe and faster-moving than other cryptocurrencies.
  • High scam overlap, including rug pulls and pump-and-dump schemes.
  • Thin liquidity, meaning it can become difficult or impossible to sell once attention fades.
  • Emotional decision-making is a particular danger here, since FOMO is often the primary driver of buying activity.

articles.title: How to Secure a Crypto Wallet
articles.description: A step-by-step checklist covering the handful of habits that prevent the vast majority of wallet theft.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What this checklist covers

This guide focuses specifically on securing a wallet you already have, whether software or hardware. If you haven't set one up yet, start with Crypto Wallets for Beginners and Hardware Wallet vs. Software Wallet first.

The core habits, in order of importance

  1. Protect your recovery phrase like it's the only copy of your life savings, because effectively, it is. Write it on paper, store it somewhere private and protected from fire and water, and never store it digitally in any form.
  2. Never enter your recovery phrase into a website, app, or message, under any circumstance. No legitimate wallet, exchange, or support agent will ever ask for it.
  3. Use a unique, strong password for every crypto-related account, ideally managed with a reputable password manager.
  4. Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere it's offered, preferring an authenticator app or hardware key over text messages. See Two-Factor Authentication, Explained.
  5. Keep your device's operating system and wallet software up to date, since updates often patch security vulnerabilities.
  6. Only install wallet apps and browser extensions from official sources, verified directly on the maker's own website, not from a search ad or a link someone sent you.

Recognizing phishing aimed at wallets

  • Fake "urgent" messages claiming your wallet needs "verification" or has a "security issue," with a link to click.
  • Fake browser extensions and apps that copy the appearance of real wallets.
  • Malicious "airdrops" that prompt you to connect your wallet and sign a transaction to claim a free token, which can secretly grant the scammer permission to move your funds.
  • Fake customer support found through search results or social media comments, rather than the official site.
Common mistake

Searching for wallet support on a general search engine and clicking the first result. Scammers buy ads and post fake "support" contacts that rank highly. Use only the official website, typed in yourself, or a link from documentation you already trust.

Managing what you've approved

When you interact with apps and smart contracts, you sometimes grant them ongoing permission to move certain tokens on your behalf. Over time, these permissions can add up, including some granted to sites you no longer use or trust.

  • Periodically review active permissions using your wallet's official tools or a reputable, well-known permission-checking tool linked from your wallet provider's own documentation.
  • Revoke permissions you no longer need, especially for apps you don't recognize or no longer use.
  • Be cautious granting broad or unlimited permissions in the first place, and prefer limiting them to the specific amount needed when an app allows it.

Everyday device habits that matter

  • Keep your phone and computer locked with a strong PIN, password, or biometric lock.
  • Avoid accessing wallets on public or shared computers.
  • Be cautious with browser extensions in general, since a malicious or compromised one could potentially interact with a wallet extension.
  • Consider a dedicated device or browser profile used only for crypto, if you hold significant amounts, to reduce exposure to unrelated malware.

Backup and recovery planning

  • Store your recovery phrase in more than one secure physical location if practical, to protect against fire, flood, or a single point of failure, while still keeping it private.
  • Consider who, if anyone, should be able to access your funds if something happened to you, and research secure inheritance options offered by reputable wallet providers, rather than sharing your phrase with anyone in advance.
  • Test your backup once, for example by restoring your wallet on a spare device using your written phrase, so you know it actually works before you truly need it.

A simple security routine

A ROUTINE WORTH KEEPING
Frequency Action
Once, at setup Write down your recovery phrase by hand; verify it; store it securely
Every few months Review and revoke unused permissions and connected apps
Whenever prompted Update wallet software and device operating system
Ongoing, every time Pause before clicking links or entering your phrase anywhere

Risks to understand

  • No checklist guarantees safety. These habits reduce risk substantially; they don't eliminate it.
  • Human error remains the biggest factor in most wallet thefts, more than any technical flaw.
  • Recovery is usually impossible once a self-custody wallet is compromised, which is why prevention matters far more here than in traditional banking.

articles.title: What Is a “Pig Butchering” Scam?
articles.description: A fast-growing and especially cruel scam pattern that often starts as a friendship or romance. Here's how to recognize it early.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it is

"Pig butchering" is the popular name for a long-running scam that combines building a personal relationship with steering the victim into a fake crypto investment. The name comes from the idea of "fattening" a victim with trust and small wins before taking everything.

The term itself can feel demeaning to people who've been targeted, and some law enforcement bodies prefer names like "romance baiting" or "investment confidence scam." You'll see all of them used.

It's one of the most damaging scams around. The FBI reported that crypto investment fraud, the category these schemes fall into, accounted for roughly $7.2 billion in reported losses in 2025.

Who it targets

Anyone. The people running these operations are organized and patient, and they use scripts and tools refined over many attempts. Victims include professionals, retirees, and people who consider themselves careful with money.

Victims are often not aware it's happening. The FBI and Secret Service ran an effort called Operation Level Up to warn victims of crypto investment scams, and about 77% of the people they contacted did not know they were being scammed.

How it usually unfolds

Every case differs, but the general shape is consistent:

  1. Contact. It often begins with something casual: a text to a "wrong number," a social media message, or a match on a dating app.
  2. Trust-building. Days or weeks of friendly, personal conversation. The person seems warm, interested, and reliable.
  3. The opportunity. Eventually, investing comes up, often framed as something they're succeeding at and want to share with you.
  4. Early "success." A fake platform shows your balance growing. You may even be allowed to withdraw a small amount, which builds confidence.
  5. Bigger deposits. You're encouraged to invest more, sometimes by borrowing or moving retirement savings.
  6. The trap. When you try to withdraw, new "fees," "taxes," or "verification payments" appear. Money sent to satisfy them is lost too.
  7. Disappearance. The friend stops replying, and the platform vanishes or locks you out.

Red flags to watch for

  • A friendly stranger who contacted you first and wants to move to a private messaging app quickly.
  • Reluctance or excuses when you suggest a live video call, or a profile that looks too polished.
  • Conversations that steadily turn toward money, crypto, or a "successful" investing method.
  • A platform or app you were pointed to, rather than one you found and researched yourself.
  • Small withdrawals that work at first, then problems once larger amounts are involved.
  • Pressure to add more money, or to keep the investment secret.
  • Extra payments demanded before you can withdraw your own money.
The key rule

Never invest through a platform recommended by someone you've only met online, no matter how well you think you know them.

How to protect yourself

  • Slow the pace. Genuine relationships don't require you to make financial decisions quickly.
  • Verify the person. Ask for a live video call, and try a reverse image search on their photos.
  • Check the platform independently. See Is This Exchange Legit? and Fake Exchange Warning Signs.
  • Tell someone you trust. Scammers often push secrecy because outside opinions break the spell.
  • Never borrow or tap retirement savings to invest in something recommended by an online contact.

If you think you're in one right now

  1. Stop sending money, including any "fee" to withdraw. It won't unlock your funds.
  2. Don't confront them. Just stop engaging and preserve everything: chats, usernames, wallet addresses, transaction IDs, and the platform's web address.
  3. Report it to the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov) and the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov).
  4. Beware of "recovery" offers that follow. See How to Recover Stolen Crypto.
  5. Talk to someone. Shame keeps many victims silent, and that silence helps the scammers.
You are not foolish

These schemes are run by organized, professional operations that are very good at what they do. Being targeted says nothing about your intelligence. If you feel overwhelmed or hopeless after a loss, in the US you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) at any time.

If someone you love may be a target

  • Stay calm and curious, not accusatory. Blame makes people defensive and secretive.
  • Ask questions like "How did you two meet?" and "Can I look at the platform with you?"
  • Show them the pattern, not just the conclusion. Sharing this guide can help.
  • Offer to help them check registration and try a small withdrawal test before anything else.

Keep in mind

  • Losses are often large because the scam is designed to keep escalating.
  • Recovery is difficult, so prevention matters far more than cure.
  • Emotional harm is real. Seek support, and don't carry this alone.

articles.title: How Does Cryptocurrency Actually Work?
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.description: The idea behind blockchains, explained without technical jargon — how a network of computers keeps track of who owns what, with no bank involved.
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The problem crypto tries to solve

When you pay for something with a card or a bank transfer, you're trusting a middleman. The bank keeps the official record of who has how much money, and everyone accepts that record because they trust the bank.

That works well most of the time. But it also means someone else is always in control: a bank can delay a payment, freeze an account, or charge a fee, and you can't check the records yourself.

Cryptocurrency was designed around a different question: can people keep an honest record of who owns what, without needing one trusted company to run it? Everything else in this guide is the answer to that question.

The big idea: a shared ledger

A ledger is just a list of transactions, like "Sam paid Priya 5 units" or "Priya paid Lee 2 units." Your bank keeps a private ledger of your account.

Now picture a shared notebook instead. Thousands of people each hold an identical copy. Whenever someone makes a payment, it gets announced to everyone, and everyone writes it into their own copy. Nobody owns the notebook, and no single copy is "the real one." If one person tried to write a fake entry, their copy would no longer match everyone else's, and it would simply be ignored.

The picture to keep in your head

A cryptocurrency is a shared notebook that thousands of computers keep in sync. The "money" isn't a physical thing or a file on your phone. It's an entry in that notebook saying that a certain address owns a certain amount.

What a blockchain actually is

A blockchain is simply the name for how that shared notebook is organized. New transactions aren't written one by one. They're collected into groups called blocks. Each block contains a batch of recent transactions, plus a kind of digital fingerprint of the block before it.

Because every block carries the fingerprint of the previous one, the blocks form a chain, in order, going back to the very first one.

BLOCK 1 Transactions + fingerprint of the start
→
BLOCK 2 Transactions + fingerprint of Block 1
→
BLOCK 3 Transactions + fingerprint of Block 2
Simplified: each block points back to the one before it, so the order can't be quietly rearranged.

Who keeps the record?

The record is kept by a network of computers, often called nodes. Anyone with the right software and an internet connection can run one. Each node stores a copy of the blockchain and checks new transactions against the rules.

This is the biggest difference from a bank. With a bank, there's one database, and the bank controls it. With a blockchain, there are thousands of copies, run by different people in different countries, and no single one of them is in charge.

BANK LEDGER

One private database, controlled by one company. You trust the company's record.

BLOCKCHAIN LEDGER

Thousands of matching copies, run by many people. You can check the record yourself.

How the network agrees on what's true

If thousands of computers each hold a copy, they need a way to agree on which new transactions are valid and in what order. This is the hardest part of the whole idea, and the method used is called a consensus mechanism. There are two main kinds you'll hear about:

  • Proof of work (used by Bitcoin): computers compete to solve a difficult puzzle, and the winner gets to add the next block. It takes real computing power and electricity, which makes cheating expensive.
  • Proof of stake (used by Ethereum and others): people lock up some of their own coins as a deposit, and the network picks who adds the next block. Dishonest behavior can cost them that deposit.

Both methods aim at the same outcome: making honesty the cheapest, easiest path and cheating costly and pointless.

Wallets and keys: how ownership works

If there's no account with your name on it, how does the network know which coins are yours? Through a pair of digital keys:

  • Public address: like an email address or bank account number. You can share it so people can send you crypto.
  • Private key: like a very long secret password. Whoever has it can spend the coins at that address.

A wallet is just the tool that stores and manages your keys and lets you sign transactions. When you "send" crypto, your wallet uses your private key to create a digital signature, which proves the request came from the owner without ever revealing the key itself.

Common mistake

Thinking your crypto is "inside" your wallet app. The coins always stay on the blockchain. Your wallet only holds the keys that prove they're yours. Lose the keys, and you lose access to the coins.

Why it's hard to cheat

Suppose someone wanted to change an old transaction, say to erase a payment they made. Because each block contains the fingerprint of the one before it, changing one old block would change its fingerprint, which would break the link to every block after it.

To pull it off, they'd have to redo the work for that block and every later block, faster than the rest of the network keeps adding new ones, while thousands of other computers keep rejecting their version. On large networks like Bitcoin, that's considered impractical. That is where the phrase "very hard to alter" comes from.

What crypto doesn't fix

Understanding how it works also means understanding where it stops working:

  • It can't tell you if something is a good idea. A transaction can be perfectly valid on the blockchain and still be a scam. The technology checks that payments follow the rules, not that the person you're paying is honest.
  • It can't undo mistakes. Send funds to the wrong address and there's no customer service department to reverse it.
  • It isn't automatically private. Most blockchains are public, so anyone can see the transactions, even if names aren't attached.
  • It isn't free of trust entirely. You still have to trust the software, the wallet you use, and any exchange you use along the way.

Risks to understand

Knowing how the technology works doesn't remove the practical risks of using it:

  • Price volatility: values can move sharply in a short time, regardless of how sound the underlying technology is.
  • No safety net: crypto holdings generally aren't insured the way bank deposits are.
  • Key loss and theft: if your private key or recovery phrase is lost or stolen, there's usually no way to recover the funds.
  • Scams: the technology being sound does not stop bad actors from using crypto's language to trick people.
  • Changing rules: regulation is still developing and can affect access, taxes, and availability.

articles.title: How to Recover Stolen Crypto
articles.description: What to actually do if you've been scammed — including the legitimate agencies to contact, and why “recovery services” advertised online are usually a second scam.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The honest truth first

Recovering stolen crypto is difficult. Transactions are hard to reverse, and scammers move funds quickly. Sometimes money can be traced and frozen, especially if it lands at a regulated exchange, but that isn't the usual outcome.

What you do in the first hours and days can make a real difference, and reporting matters even if you don't expect to get money back.

The first hour: steps to take now

  1. Stop sending money. That includes "fees" or "taxes" to release funds. They're part of the scam.
  2. Secure your accounts. From a device you trust, change passwords for your email, exchange, and any related accounts, and turn on two-factor authentication.
  3. If a wallet or recovery phrase may be compromised, create a brand-new wallet and move remaining funds there right away.
  4. Write everything down. Wallet addresses, transaction IDs, dates, amounts, website addresses, usernames, emails, phone numbers, and screenshots of conversations.
  5. Contact any exchange or payment company involved. If funds went through one, tell its fraud team immediately, since they may be able to flag or freeze them.
  6. Contact your bank or card issuer if you used a bank transfer, card, or payment app. Ask about reversing or disputing the payment.

Who to report to

OFFICIAL REPORTING CHANNELS
Agency What it's for Where
FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) Internet and crypto fraud ic3.gov
Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Scams and fraud reports ReportFraud.ftc.gov
SEC Investment fraud and unregistered offerings sec.gov/tcr
CFTC Commodity and derivatives fraud cftc.gov (file a complaint)
State attorney general or securities regulator Local enforcement and consumer help Search your state's official site
Local police Creates an official case number, useful for banks and insurers Your local department
IdentityTheft.gov (FTC) If personal information or identity was stolen IdentityTheft.gov
Always type these addresses yourself. Don't follow links sent to you by strangers, and confirm current contact details on each agency's own site.

The second scam: "recovery services"

After a loss, victims are often targeted again. This is extremely common. People or companies appear, sometimes by message, sometimes in search ads or social media comments, claiming they can trace and retrieve your crypto.

  • They demand payment first, often called a "retrieval fee," "legal fee," "tax," or "gas."
  • They guarantee results. No one can honestly guarantee a recovery.
  • They contact you first, or claim to be a hacker, government official, or lawyer who "found" your case.
  • They ask for your recovery phrase or remote access to your device.
  • They pose as agencies and use official-looking names and logos.
Important

Legitimate government agencies do not charge you to take a report or help pursue a case. Some real attorneys and blockchain-analysis firms do offer services, but check credentials independently, never pay large sums upfront for a guaranteed outcome, and never share your phrase.

What to realistically expect

  • Investigations take time, often months or longer, and outcomes vary widely.
  • You may not get a personal update from every agency, even when your report is useful.
  • Recovery is possible in some cases, particularly when funds are frozen at a regulated platform, but it's never guaranteed.
  • Losses may have tax implications. Keep your records and speak with a qualified tax professional.

Looking after yourself

A financial loss like this can bring shame, anger, and anxiety. Those feelings are normal, and they're not a sign you were careless.

You are not foolish

These schemes are run by organized, professional operations that are very good at what they do. Being targeted says nothing about your intelligence. If you feel overwhelmed or hopeless after a loss, in the US you can call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) at any time.

Making sure it doesn't happen again

  • Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere. See Two-Factor Authentication, Explained.
  • Use a unique password for every account, with a password manager.
  • Learn the warning signs in How to Spot a Crypto Scam.
  • Never share your recovery phrase with anyone.

Keep in mind

  • There's no guarantee of recovery, however quickly you act.
  • Second-wave scams target victims specifically.
  • Details change. Confirm current reporting steps on the agencies' own websites.

articles.title: Slippage
articles.description: The difference between the price you expected for a trade and the price you actually got, usually caused by fast-moving markets.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

Slippage is the gap between the price you expected to pay or receive for a trade and the price you actually got once the trade completed. For example, if you expect to buy a token at $10 but the trade actually executes at $10.30, that $0.30 difference is slippage.

Why it happens

Prices can move in the brief moment between when you submit a trade and when it actually executes, especially during periods of high volatility or heavy trading activity. On decentralized exchanges specifically, slippage can also happen because a trade itself uses up some of the available funds in a trading pool, shifting the price as the trade executes, particularly for larger trades relative to that pool's size.

A simple way to think about it

The price you see before confirming a trade is a snapshot, not a guarantee. By the time your trade actually goes through, especially during a busy or fast-moving moment, the real price can have shifted slightly, or sometimes significantly.

Why liquidity makes such a big difference

Liquidity refers to how much trading activity and available funds exist for a given asset. Highly liquid assets, with lots of buyers and sellers active at once, tend to have low slippage under normal conditions. Thinly traded assets, with little activity, can experience much larger slippage, since even a moderately sized trade can meaningfully move the price.

Common mistake

Placing a large trade on a small, low-liquidity token and being surprised by a much worse price than expected. The token's price chart alone doesn't show you how thin the actual trading activity behind it is.

Slippage tolerance settings

Many decentralized exchanges let you set a slippage tolerance, a maximum percentage difference you're willing to accept between the expected and final price. If the price moves beyond that tolerance before your trade executes, the trade is cancelled rather than completed at a worse price than you specified.

  • Setting it too low can cause trades to fail repeatedly during volatile periods, since almost any price movement exceeds your limit.
  • Setting it too high can expose you to a much worse price than expected, particularly on illiquid tokens, in exchange for a trade that reliably goes through.

Risks to understand

  • Slippage can meaningfully affect what you actually pay or receive, beyond what a listed price alone suggests.
  • It tends to be worse during high volatility or for less liquid, smaller tokens.
  • Setting a slippage tolerance involves a real trade-off between reliability and price protection, with no universally correct setting.

articles.title: Crypto Tax-Loss Harvesting
articles.description: A legitimate, IRS-recognized strategy some investors use around year-end — explained plainly, with its real limitations.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What tax-loss harvesting is

Tax-loss harvesting means deliberately selling an investment that's currently worth less than you paid for it, in order to "realize" that loss for tax purposes. That realized loss can then be used to offset capital gains elsewhere, potentially reducing your overall tax bill for the year.

This is a widely used, entirely legitimate strategy across many types of investments, not something specific or unique to crypto.

How the offset actually works

  • Losses first offset gains of the same type. Short-term losses offset short-term gains; long-term losses offset long-term gains, generally speaking.
  • Leftover losses can offset the other type of gain. If losses exceed gains of the same type, they can generally offset the other category too.
  • Extra losses can offset a limited amount of ordinary income. Currently, up to $3,000 per year ($1,500 if married filing separately) of net capital losses can offset other income, such as wages.
  • Losses beyond that can typically be carried forward to future tax years, subject to current rules.

The wash sale rule, and why it currently doesn't apply to crypto

For stocks and securities, the wash sale rule (IRC Section 1091) disallows a tax loss if you sell an asset at a loss and then buy back the same or a "substantially identical" asset within 30 days before or after the sale. It exists to prevent people from claiming a tax loss while never actually changing their investment position.

Because the IRS currently classifies crypto as property rather than a "security," the wash sale rule does not currently apply to cryptocurrency. This means it's currently possible to sell a crypto asset at a loss and immediately repurchase the same asset, while still claiming the tax loss, something that would not be allowed with a stock.

Important caveat

This is current law, not a permanent feature of the tax code. Congress has discussed extending wash sale-style rules to cover digital assets, and this is an area of active legislative attention. Confirm current rules for the specific tax year you're filing, since this could change.

A simplified, hypothetical example

Say you bought 1 unit of a coin for $10,000, and it's now worth $6,000. You could sell it, realizing a $4,000 loss, and immediately buy back the same amount of the same coin at the current $6,000 price.

HYPOTHETICAL EXAMPLE — ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY
Step Amount
Original cost basis $10,000
Value at time of sale $6,000
Realized capital loss $4,000
New cost basis after repurchasing immediately $6,000
Made-up figures for illustration only, not a projection or recommendation.

You'd still hold the same amount of the same coin afterward, but you've realized a loss that can now be used against gains elsewhere, while your cost basis resets lower for future calculations.

Real limitations worth understanding

  • It doesn't create money from nothing. You're realizing an actual loss on an asset that actually declined in value; it's a timing and tax-treatment tool, not a way to profit from a loss itself.
  • Transaction costs still apply. Trading fees on the sale and repurchase reduce the practical benefit, especially for frequent, small-scale harvesting.
  • Rules can change, including the wash sale treatment discussed above, which is an active area of legislative discussion.
  • It doesn't change your overall investment view. If you didn't actually want to hold the asset anymore, harvesting a loss and immediately repurchasing may not make sense in the first place.
  • Complexity grows with frequency. Harvesting losses across many small positions increases record-keeping and reporting complexity covered in IRS Crypto Tax Form 8949.

When people typically consider this

This is most commonly discussed near year-end, when investors review realized and unrealized gains and losses for the year and consider whether locking in a loss makes sense before December 31, the general cutoff for a given tax year. This is exactly the kind of decision worth discussing directly with a tax professional, since it depends on your full financial picture, not just one position.

Keep in mind

  • This is a tax timing strategy, not an investment strategy. It doesn't change whether the underlying asset is a good idea to hold.
  • The lack of a crypto wash sale rule could change in a future tax year.
  • Poorly executed harvesting, without considering fees and your actual investment goals, can cost more than it saves.

articles.title: Are NFTs Still a Thing?
articles.description: A fair, updated look at what NFTs are actually used for today, separate from the hype cycle a few years back.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The short answer

Yes, NFTs still exist and are still actively traded and built on, but the market looks very different from its 2021 peak. Trading volumes and prices for most NFT collections have fallen sharply since then, while some specific use cases have kept developing quietly.

If your picture of NFTs is frozen at "everyone was buying expensive cartoon profile pictures," that period has largely passed. What's left is a smaller, more specialized set of uses.

A quick reminder of what an NFT is

NFT stands for "non-fungible token." "Fungible" means interchangeable, like a dollar bill, where any one is as good as another. "Non-fungible" means unique: each NFT is a distinct entry recorded on a blockchain, often pointing to a specific piece of digital art, a collectible, or another item.

Common mistake

Believing you legally own the underlying artwork, its copyright, or exclusive rights to it just by owning the NFT. In most cases, you own a blockchain record pointing to the file, not the copyright itself, unless the project specifically grants you additional rights in writing.

What happened to the hype cycle

Between 2021 and early 2022, NFT trading volumes and some individual sale prices reached levels that later proved unsustainable. Prices for many popular collections fell sharply afterward, and trading volume across the NFT market as a whole declined substantially from its peak.

Some of that activity was later found to involve wash trading, where the same or related parties trade an asset back and forth to inflate its apparent volume or price. This inflated how active and valuable the market appeared to be during the peak.

What NFTs are actually used for today

  • Digital art and collectibles, a smaller but still active market for established and emerging artists.
  • Gaming items, such as in-game assets that players can own and sometimes trade, on platforms that support it.
  • Event tickets and access passes, using an NFT to verify a ticket or membership rather than a traditional paper or app-based ticket.
  • Real-world asset records, some pilot projects use NFTs or similar tokens to represent ownership records for things like real estate shares or collectibles, though this remains an early and developing use case.
  • Music and royalties, some artists have experimented with NFTs tied to music rights or fan access.

These uses are narrower and more specific than the broad speculative buying that characterized the earlier hype period.

Risks that are specific to NFTs

  • Illiquidity. Unlike a widely traded coin, a specific NFT may have no buyers at all when you want to sell, regardless of the price you set.
  • Valuation is highly subjective, often based on trends and community sentiment rather than any underlying cash flow or asset.
  • Wash trading and fake volume can make a collection look more active or valuable than it really is.
  • Smart contract and platform risk, similar to other crypto assets, including hacks of NFT marketplaces or minting sites.
  • Copyright confusion, as covered above, regarding what you actually own.
  • Scams targeting buyers, including fake collections, phishing sites mimicking real marketplaces, and "rug pull" style projects that disappear after minting. See Crypto Rug Pull, Meaning.

A fair way to think about it now

NFTs are technology, a way of recording unique ownership on a blockchain, separate from any particular use of that technology. The 2021 hype cycle was about one narrow application, speculative profile-picture collections, not about the underlying idea itself.

Some real, useful applications appear to be developing more quietly, while much of the earlier speculative activity has faded. Whether any specific NFT or platform is a reasonable use of your money is a separate question from whether NFTs "still exist," and depends entirely on the specific project.

articles.title: What Is an Altcoin?
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.description: A simple definition of the thousands of cryptocurrencies that aren't Bitcoin, and why “different” doesn't mean “better” or “worse.”
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What "altcoin" means

Altcoin is short for "alternative coin," and it simply refers to any cryptocurrency that isn't Bitcoin. By that definition, Ethereum is technically an altcoin too, even though it's huge in its own right. The term is really just a way of separating "Bitcoin" from "everything else."

There are thousands of altcoins, ranging from large, well-established projects to tiny, untested ones created days ago.

Why so many exist

Because blockchain technology is open, anyone with the right skills can create a new cryptocurrency. People create altcoins for very different reasons:

  • Trying a different technical approach, such as faster transactions or lower fees.
  • Building a specific application, like a coin used inside a particular game or platform.
  • Genuine experimentation by developers exploring new ideas.
  • Pure speculation or promotion, created mainly to attract buyers with little underlying substance.
  • Fraud, created specifically to take investors' money. See Crypto Rug Pull, Meaning.

All of these can look similar from a website or a social media post. The reason behind a coin's existence isn't visible on the surface.

Broad categories you'll come across

COMMON TYPES
Category General idea
Smart contract platforms Networks like Ethereum built to run applications, not just move a currency
Stablecoins Designed to hold a steady value. See What Is a Stablecoin?
Utility tokens Meant to be used within a specific platform or service, such as paying network fees
Governance tokens Give holders a vote in decisions about how a project is run
Memecoins Often created around a joke or internet trend, usually with little stated purpose. See Memecoin Risk, Explained
Simplified categories. Many projects blend more than one of these.

Why "different" doesn't mean "better" or "worse"

A common beginner mistake is assuming a newer or cheaper-per-coin altcoin is automatically a better deal than a more expensive, established one, or that an older coin is automatically safer just because it's been around longer.

Common mistake

Confusing a low price per coin with being "cheap" or a good value. Price per coin depends on how many total coins exist, which tells you nothing on its own about whether the project is sound.

Every altcoin needs to be evaluated on its own, based on what it actually does, who's behind it, how widely it's used, and how transparent the team is, not on price alone or how new and exciting it seems.

A basic way to think about evaluating one

  • What problem does it claim to solve, and does that explanation make sense in plain language?
  • Is there a real, working product, or only promises and a roadmap?
  • Who's behind it? Named, verifiable people and organizations are a better sign than anonymous teams.
  • How concentrated is ownership? A blockchain explorer can show whether a small number of wallets hold most of the supply.
  • How is it talked about? Heavy hype and guaranteed-return language are warning signs, covered fully in How to Spot a Crypto Scam.

This guide gives you a way to think it through. It isn't a recommendation of any specific coin, and we don't rank or endorse any.

Risks to understand

  • Most altcoins carry higher risk than Bitcoin or Ethereum, simply from being smaller, newer, and less tested.
  • Many altcoins fail completely and lose all their value over time.
  • Liquidity can be thin, meaning it can be hard to sell without moving the price significantly.
  • Information is often one-sided, coming mainly from the project's own promotion.
  • Regulation varies and continues to evolve, which can affect access or legality.

articles.title: Do I Have to Report Crypto on My Taxes?
articles.description: A direct answer, with the specific situations where reporting is required — including ones people often miss.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The short answer

Yes, almost certainly, if you've done anything with crypto beyond simply buying it with dollars and holding it untouched. The specifics depend on what you actually did, covered below.

The digital asset question on your tax return

Every federal income tax return now includes a direct yes-or-no question near the top of Form 1040, asking whether, at any time during the year, you received digital assets as a reward, award, or payment, or sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of a digital asset.

Important

Answer this question honestly and completely. It applies broadly, and answering "no" when the true answer is "yes" is treated seriously, independent of whether tax was actually owed on the underlying activity.

Situations that require reporting

  • Selling crypto for US dollars, at a gain or a loss. Losses generally still need to be reported.
  • Trading one cryptocurrency for another, even if you never converted to dollars. See Is a Crypto-to-Crypto Trade Taxable?
  • Using crypto to pay for goods or services. This is treated as a disposal of the crypto, at its value at the time.
  • Receiving crypto as payment for work, whether as an employee or a contractor.
  • Mining or staking rewards.
  • Airdrops and hard fork proceeds you received and had the ability to control or transfer.
  • Receiving crypto as a gift, in some situations, once you eventually sell or dispose of it, since you generally inherit the giver's original cost basis.

Situations people often overlook

  • Small purchases made with crypto. Buying a cup of coffee with crypto is technically a taxable disposal, even for a tiny amount. Many people don't realize this applies to everyday purchases, not just large investment sales.
  • Swapping tokens inside a decentralized exchange (DEX) or DeFi app. These often don't generate any tax form at all, but the reporting obligation still applies.
  • NFT sales and trades, which follow similar disposal principles.
  • Receiving free tokens through a promotion or airdrop that you didn't specifically request.
  • Interest or rewards earned through crypto lending or "savings" products, generally treated as ordinary income when received.
  • Losses. Some people assume that if they lost money, there's nothing to report. Losses generally still need to be reported, and doing so may actually reduce your tax bill through the strategies covered in Crypto Tax-Loss Harvesting.

Why "I didn't get a form" isn't an excuse

The IRS has explicitly stated that taxpayers must report digital asset transactions whether or not a 1099 form was received. Many activities, including most DeFi transactions, wallet-to-wallet activity across different platforms, and peer-to-peer transfers, currently fall outside mandatory broker reporting entirely.

That gap in third-party reporting does not create a gap in your own obligation to report. It just means you're more likely to be personally responsible for keeping the records.

When you generally don't need to report anything new

  • Buying crypto with US dollars and simply holding it, with no sale, trade, or spending.
  • Moving crypto between wallets you own and control yourself, though you still need to track cost basis accurately for when you eventually do sell.

If you haven't been reporting crypto and should have

If you realize past returns were incomplete, options generally exist to correct this, including filing an amended return. This is a genuinely useful conversation to have directly with a qualified tax professional, since the right approach depends on your specific history and amounts involved, which this guide can't assess for you.

Keep in mind

  • Reporting requirements are broad and cover far more situations than most beginners expect.
  • The IRS's visibility into crypto activity has increased substantially with Form 1099-DA.
  • When in doubt, report it, or ask a tax professional, rather than assuming a small or informal transaction doesn't count.

articles.title: Crypto Giveaway Scams
articles.description: Why “send 1 to get 2 back” offers — even ones appearing to come from celebrities — are always fake, no exceptions.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What a giveaway scam is

A crypto giveaway scam promises to multiply the crypto you send, or to reward you for taking part. The classic version says something like "send one coin to this address and get two back."

It usually appears to come from someone famous or a well-known company, which is exactly why people trust it.

Why they are always fake

  • Real giveaways never require you to pay first. A genuine prize doesn't cost the winner money.
  • The math doesn't work. Nobody can "multiply" money sent to an address. The sender keeps nothing, and the address belongs to the scammer.
  • Crypto transfers can't be undone. Once it's sent, it's gone.
  • Real projects have no reason to ask for your wallet keys or recovery phrase.
The simple rule

If an offer needs you to send crypto to receive crypto, it is a scam. There is no exception.

How they usually appear

  • Hacked or lookalike accounts. Verified accounts get taken over, or fake accounts imitate real ones and reply under genuine posts.
  • Fake livestreams and videos. Reused footage or AI-generated faces and voices of famous people, with a QR code or link on screen.
  • Lookalike websites with countdown timers and "claim now" buttons.
  • Wallet-connect traps. A site asks you to connect your wallet and approve a transaction that can quietly give it permission to move your tokens.
  • Direct messages saying you've "won" something you never entered.
Common mistake

Trusting a blue verification badge. Accounts can be hacked, badges can be bought, and lookalike names can be very convincing. A badge isn't proof of a real giveaway.

Rules that keep you safe

  1. Never send crypto to receive crypto.
  2. Never share your recovery phrase or private key, with anyone, for any reason.
  3. Don't connect your wallet to unfamiliar sites or approve transactions you don't understand.
  4. Verify through official channels. Type the company's real web address yourself and look for the announcement there.
  5. Be suspicious of urgency like countdown timers and "first 100 people only."
  6. Block and report the account or video on the platform where you saw it.

If you sent money or connected your wallet

  • Stop. Don't send anything more, including "fees" to release a prize.
  • If you only sent crypto, it's very likely gone, but report it and keep all the details (address, transaction ID, the page or account).
  • If you connected your wallet or approved something, consider moving your remaining funds to a brand-new wallet with a new recovery phrase, and consider revoking permissions using your wallet's official tools.
  • Report it to the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov) and the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov).
If you've already sent money

Stop sending anything further, keep every record, and read How to Recover Stolen Crypto for the exact steps and the agencies to contact. Acting quickly can matter.

Keep in mind

  • Deepfakes are getting better. A convincing video is not evidence.
  • Loss is usually permanent. Prevention is the only reliable protection.
  • Genuine promotions exist (for example, ordinary marketing contests), but they never ask you to send crypto or share keys.

articles.title: Difference Between a Coin and a Token
articles.description: A common point of confusion, cleared up in under two minutes of reading.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

The short version

A coin has its own independent blockchain. A token is built on top of someone else's blockchain, using that network's existing rules.

That's the entire technical distinction. Everything else, price, purpose, popularity, is separate from this and doesn't change which category something falls into.

What makes something a coin

Bitcoin is a coin because it has its own dedicated blockchain, built specifically to track bitcoin transactions. Ethereum's own currency, ETH, is a coin for the same reason: it runs on Ethereum's own blockchain, which Ethereum itself maintains.

Generally, if a cryptocurrency has its own independent network of computers verifying its own transactions, it's a coin.

What makes something a token

A token doesn't have its own blockchain. Instead, it's created using a set of rules, called a standard, on top of an existing network, most commonly Ethereum. A well-known example is the ERC-20 standard, a common template developers use to create tokens on Ethereum.

Practically, this means a token relies on the host blockchain, most often Ethereum, to process its transactions, while the project behind the token only controls what the token itself does, not the underlying network.

A simple analogy

Think of a coin's blockchain as its own country with its own currency and government. A token is more like a business operating inside a country, using that country's roads, laws, and currency system rather than building its own.

Why the distinction actually matters

  • Fees. Sending a token usually still requires paying a fee in the host blockchain's own coin, for example ETH, even though you're sending a different token.
  • Two layers of risk. A token depends on both the underlying blockchain working correctly and the token's own project code being sound. A coin only depends on its own network.
  • Wallet compatibility. Wallets that support a blockchain, like Ethereum, generally can hold many different tokens built on it, not just its native coin.
  • What a failure actually affects. If Ethereum itself had a serious problem, it could affect every token built on it. A problem with one specific token's project usually doesn't affect Ethereum or other unrelated tokens.

Where people get confused

  • Everyday language. Most people say "coin" for any cryptocurrency, tokens included. That's fine in casual conversation, but it isn't the technical definition.
  • Wrapped assets. Sometimes a coin from one blockchain is represented as a token on another, to make it usable there. The original coin and its wrapped token version are related but not identical, and each carries its own risks.
  • Native currency versus a project's own token. A blockchain's own coin (like ETH on Ethereum) is different from a token that some other project chooses to build on that same blockchain.

A quick way to check which one you're looking at

  1. Look up whether the asset has "its own blockchain" or is described as being built "on" another network.
  2. Check whether it needs a separate coin (like ETH) to pay network fees, a sign it's a token.
  3. Search the project's own documentation or whitepaper, which will usually state this directly.

Risks to understand

  • Token projects can fail independently of the blockchain they're built on.
  • Smart contract bugs in a token's code can lead to loss of funds, separate from the host network's security.
  • Network congestion or high fees on the host blockchain can affect every token built on it at once.
  • Being "just a token" isn't automatically riskier than being a coin. Many small, independent coins carry just as much or more risk.

articles.title: IRS Crypto Tax Form 8949
articles.description: A walkthrough of the actual form used to report crypto transactions, explained without accountant jargon.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What Form 8949 is for

Form 8949, "Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets," is where you list the details of each individual sale or trade of a capital asset, crypto included. Its totals then flow into Schedule D, which summarizes your overall capital gains and losses for the year on your tax return.

Think of Form 8949 as the detailed transaction log, and Schedule D as the summary page built from it.

The information each line needs

For every crypto disposal, generally speaking you'll need:

WHAT GOES ON EACH LINE
Field What it means
Description of property Which cryptocurrency and roughly how much, for example "0.25 BTC"
Date acquired When you originally obtained that specific crypto
Date sold or disposed When you sold, traded, or spent it
Proceeds What you received in return, valued in US dollars at the time
Cost basis What you originally paid for it, including fees, in US dollars
Gain or loss Proceeds minus cost basis

Why there are different "boxes" (categories) on the form

Form 8949 separates transactions into different sections, mainly based on how the transaction was reported to the IRS and whether it was short-term or long-term:

  • Short-term vs. long-term: based on whether you held the asset for one year or less, or more than one year, which affects the tax rate as covered in How Is Cryptocurrency Taxed in the US?
  • Whether basis was reported to the IRS by a broker: transactions where an exchange sent the IRS your cost basis information (via Form 1099-DA) generally go in a different category than ones where you're reporting basis yourself, since exchanges aren't required to report basis for every type of transaction.

Crypto tax software or a tax professional can help sort your transactions into the correct categories; the form's own instructions explain the exact category codes if you're completing it by hand.

How Form 1099-DA connects to this

If a centralized exchange issued you a Form 1099-DA, it will show gross proceeds, and for certain covered transactions, cost basis information, that the exchange also sent to the IRS. You'll generally still need to list these transactions individually on Form 8949, cross-checked against the 1099-DA.

Common mistake

Assuming the exchange's reported cost basis is automatically correct and complete. If you transferred crypto into that exchange from elsewhere, moved it between wallets, or the exchange lacks full history, its cost basis figure may be inaccurate or missing entirely. Keep your own independent records to verify against.

What Form 1099-DA generally won't cover

Activity outside centralized exchanges, including most decentralized finance (DeFi) transactions, wallet-to-wallet transfers between different platforms, and peer-to-peer trades, typically isn't captured on a 1099-DA at all. If you engaged in any of this, you're responsible for compiling those transaction details yourself for Form 8949.

How it flows into the rest of your return

  1. List each disposal individually on Form 8949, in the correct short-term or long-term section.
  2. Total each section's gains and losses.
  3. Transfer those totals to the corresponding lines on Schedule D.
  4. Schedule D combines everything into your overall net capital gain or loss, which then flows into your Form 1040.

Making this manageable

  • Crypto tax software can import exchange and wallet data and generate a completed Form 8949 automatically, which is far more practical than hand-tracking dozens or hundreds of transactions.
  • A tax professional experienced with digital assets can review software-generated output and catch gaps, particularly around DeFi activity or multiple wallets.
  • Keep your own transaction records year-round, rather than trying to reconstruct a full year of activity in April.

Keep in mind

  • Missing or incorrect entries can lead to over- or under-reporting your actual tax liability.
  • Manually completing this form for high transaction volumes is genuinely difficult without software.
  • The form and its instructions can change between tax years; always use the current version from irs.gov.

articles.title: Seed Phrase
articles.description: A list of 12–24 random words that acts as the master password to a crypto wallet. Lose it, and there's usually no way to recover your funds.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

A seed phrase, also called a recovery phrase, is a list of usually 12 or 24 plain English words, generated randomly when you set up a crypto wallet. It can restore your entire wallet, and every key inside it, on a brand-new device if your original one is lost, stolen, or broken.

Why it exists, and why it's so powerful

Wallets need a backup method, since there's no company to call for a password reset in self-custody. A seed phrase solves that by being a single, human-readable backup for something that's normally an impossibly long string of random characters.

The trade-off is that this convenience cuts both ways: whoever has your seed phrase has full access to your funds, with no additional password or approval required in most cases.

What one actually looks like

A seed phrase looks something like this (this is a made-up, unused example, never a real wallet):

Example only — never a real wallet

witch collapse practice feed shine open despair creek road again ice least

A real phrase would be generated randomly by your own wallet software during setup, never given to you by someone else, and never something you'd choose yourself.

How to handle one correctly

  • Write it on paper, by hand, as soon as your wallet generates it.
  • Store it somewhere private, protected from fire, water, and other people finding it.
  • Never store it digitally, not in a photo, a notes app, an email, or cloud storage of any kind.
  • Never type it into a website, app, or message, no matter who is asking or how official they seem.
Common mistake

Entering a seed phrase into a website to "verify" or "validate" a wallet. This is one of the most common ways people lose everything. See the full checklist in How to Secure a Crypto Wallet.

Risks to understand

  • Losing it usually means losing access permanently, with no "forgot password" option.
  • Anyone who obtains it can take everything, instantly and irreversibly.
  • It's the single most valuable piece of information in self-custody crypto, worth treating with more care than a bank PIN or password.

articles.title: Hardware Wallet vs. Software Wallet
articles.description: A practical comparison of the two main ways to hold your own crypto, including cost and convenience differences.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

A quick recap

Both hardware and software wallets are ways to hold your own private keys, the self-custody option covered in Self-Custody vs. Exchange Custody. The difference between them is simply where those keys physically live.

What a software wallet is

A software wallet is an app, on your phone, computer, or as a browser extension, that stores your keys digitally on that device. It's connected to the internet whenever the app is open, which is why this category is often called a hot wallet.

  • Cost: free, in almost all cases.
  • Convenience: high. Easy to install, easy to use for frequent transactions.
  • Main risk: anything that compromises the device, malware, phishing, or a stolen and unlocked phone, can potentially expose the keys.

What a hardware wallet is

A hardware wallet is a small, dedicated physical device built specifically to generate and store private keys offline. To approve a transaction, you connect it to a phone or computer and confirm the action directly on the device itself, which is why this category is often called a cold wallet.

Because the keys never leave the device and aren't exposed to your internet-connected computer or phone, hardware wallets are widely considered the strongest practical protection against remote hacking for individual users.

  • Cost: typically a one-time purchase, usually in the range of $50 to $250 depending on the model and features, though prices and options change, so check current pricing directly from the manufacturer.
  • Convenience: lower. You need the physical device on hand to approve transactions, which adds a small amount of friction.
  • Main risk: losing the device or its backup phrase, or buying a device that's been tampered with before it reached you.

Side by side

COMPARISON
Software wallet Hardware wallet
Typical cost Free One-time purchase, roughly $50–$250
Where keys are stored On your phone or computer (online) On a dedicated offline device
Convenience High; good for frequent use Lower; best for less frequent access
Exposure to online attacks Higher, since the device is internet-connected Much lower, since keys stay offline
Good fit for Smaller, actively used amounts Larger amounts held for longer periods

How to think about which one to use

Many people don't pick just one. A common, reasonable approach:

  • Software wallet for a smaller amount you use regularly, similar to cash you'd carry day to day.
  • Hardware wallet for larger or long-term holdings, similar to savings you don't need to access often.
A simple way to frame it

The more an amount would hurt to lose, and the less often you need to touch it, the stronger the case for moving it to a hardware wallet.

Buying a hardware wallet safely

  • Buy directly from the manufacturer's official website, not from a general marketplace or a reseller, where a device could be intercepted and tampered with before shipping.
  • Check the packaging for tamper-evidence the manufacturer describes on its own site.
  • Generate your recovery phrase yourself, on the device, during setup. Never use a device that arrives with a phrase already written down or preprinted; that's a sign it may be compromised.
  • Keep firmware updated using only the manufacturer's official app or website.

Risks to understand

  • Software wallets are more exposed to malware and phishing, since they run on general-purpose, internet-connected devices.
  • Hardware wallets can still be lost, damaged, or stolen, and the recovery phrase remains the ultimate backup either way.
  • A tampered device is a real risk if bought from an unofficial source.
  • Neither type protects you from sending funds to the wrong address or from approving a malicious transaction you didn't fully understand.

articles.title: Gas Fee
articles.description: The cost charged to process a transaction on certain blockchains, similar in idea to a transaction or processing fee.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

A gas fee is the cost paid to have a transaction processed and confirmed on certain blockchains, most notably Ethereum and similar networks. The term comes from the idea of "fuel" needed to run the computation that processes your transaction.

Every action on these networks, sending funds, trading tokens, or interacting with an application, requires some amount of gas, paid in that network's own native coin.

Why gas fees exist

Processing a transaction takes real computing resources from the computers maintaining the network, as explained in How Does Cryptocurrency Actually Work? Gas fees compensate the network for that work and also help prevent people from spamming the network with pointless transactions, since every single action has a real cost attached.

Why gas fees change constantly

Gas fees aren't fixed. They rise and fall based on how much demand there is for space on the network at any given moment, similar to surge pricing. During periods of high activity, fees can rise sharply; during quiet periods, they can be quite low.

A simple way to think about it

Gas fees work like a busy toll road. During rush hour, more people want to use the same limited space, and the price to get through goes up. Off-peak, it's cheaper.

Why this matters practically

  • Small transactions can become disproportionately expensive during high-demand periods, since the fee doesn't scale down for a smaller amount.
  • Frequent trading or DeFi activity can add up in fees over time, an easy detail to overlook when estimating returns.
  • Setting a fee too low during high demand can leave a transaction stuck for a long time rather than failing cleanly.
Common mistake

Forgetting to account for gas fees when calculating whether a small trade or transfer is actually worth doing. On a busy network, the fee alone can exceed the value of a very small transaction.

Risks to understand

  • Fees are unpredictable and can spike quickly during high demand.
  • A stuck transaction can be confusing for beginners to resolve, and specific fixes vary by wallet and network.
  • Fees vary significantly between different blockchains, so "high gas fees" isn't true of every network at all times.
