articles.title: Whitepaper
articles.description: A document a crypto project publishes explaining what it does and how it works, similar to a business plan. Worth reading before trusting a claim about a coin.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written by the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What it means

A whitepaper is a document a crypto project publishes to explain its purpose, how its technology works, and often details like its total coin supply and how new coins are distributed. It plays a role similar to a business plan or a technical proposal, aimed at both potential users and investors.

The most famous example is Bitcoin's own whitepaper, published in 2008, which introduced its design to the world before the network even launched.

What a whitepaper typically covers

  • The problem the project claims to solve.
  • How the technology works, at some level of technical detail.
  • Tokenomics: total supply, how coins are distributed, and to whom.
  • The team behind the project, ideally with verifiable names and backgrounds.
  • A roadmap of planned future development.

Why it's worth reading before trusting a claim

A whitepaper is one of the few places a project has to make its actual case in some detail, rather than through a short social media post or an influencer's endorsement. Reading it, even without deep technical knowledge, can reveal a lot: whether the explanation actually makes sense, whether the team is named and verifiable, and whether the numbers around token distribution raise any concerns.

How to read one critically, without needing to be a programmer

  1. Can you explain the core idea back in plain English after reading it? If the whitepaper is all jargon with no clear plain-language explanation anywhere, that's worth noting.
  2. Are the team members named, and can you verify them independently, outside of the project's own website?
  3. How is the token supply distributed? A very large share reserved for the founding team or early insiders is worth extra scrutiny.
  4. Does it sound original, or does it closely resemble another project's language and structure?
  5. Does it make specific, falsifiable claims, or mostly vague promises and excitement?
Common mistake

Treating the mere existence of a whitepaper as a stamp of legitimacy. Plenty of failed and fraudulent projects have published professional-looking whitepapers. It's a starting point for research, not a conclusion.

Risks to understand

  • A whitepaper can be entirely aspirational, describing a product that's never actually built.
  • Technical language can be used to obscure, rather than clarify, a weak or dishonest underlying plan.
  • Whitepapers are self-published by the project itself, with no independent review requirement, unlike a prospectus for a registered security.

articles.description: A plain definition of one of the most common ways new tokens collapse, and the signs that usually show up beforehand.
articles.title: Crypto Rug Pull, Meaning
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

What "rug pull" means

A rug pull is when the people behind a crypto project attract money from investors and then abruptly take that money out, leaving the token worthless. The name comes from the phrase "pulling the rug out from under someone."

It usually happens fast. One day a token is being heavily promoted and its price is climbing, and the next, the price drops to almost nothing and the creators have disappeared.

Why it's so easy to do

On many blockchains, anyone can create a new token in minutes and list it for trading, with little or no review. That openness is part of what makes crypto interesting, but it also means there's no gatekeeper checking whether a new token is real.

Scammers count on that. They can create a token, generate excitement, wait for people to buy, and leave with the proceeds.

The general forms it takes

Without going into how any of it is done, it helps to recognize the outcomes:

  • Pulled funds. The creators drain the money that investors put in, so there is nothing left to trade against.
  • Insider dumping. People holding a large share of the supply sell it all at once after the price has been pushed up.
  • Blocked selling. The token is built so ordinary buyers can buy but can't sell, while insiders can.
  • Slow fade. The team stops working, stops communicating, and the project quietly dies. This can be a scam or just a failure, and the result for investors is the same.

Warning signs that often show up beforehand

  • Anonymous team. No real names, no verifiable track record, or fake profile photos.
  • Heavy hype, thin substance. Lots of excitement, memes, and influencer promotion, but no working product or clear purpose.
  • Concentrated ownership. A small number of wallets holding most of the supply. A blockchain explorer can show this.
  • Unclear or absent information about how the money is secured and whether creators can withdraw it.
  • Promises of huge or guaranteed returns.
  • Copied or unexplained materials, such as a whitepaper or website that looks copied from another project.
  • Pressure and urgency: "buy now before it pumps."
  • Problems selling. Users complaining they can't sell or are hit with huge fees.
  • Sudden changes, like deleted social accounts, disabled comments, or a silent community chat.
Common mistake

Assuming a project is safe because it has an "audit" badge or says liquidity is "locked." These can be helpful signals but aren't guarantees. Audits vary widely in quality, and badges can be faked.

Rug pull vs. a bad investment

The difference is intent. A rug pull is deliberate fraud, while a failed project may just be a bad idea, poor execution, or bad luck. From the outside it's often hard to tell them apart, and your loss is the same either way.

Rug pulls can be illegal fraud, and authorities have prosecuted some cases, but recovering money is difficult once it's moved.

Habits that reduce your risk

  • Be very cautious with brand-new tokens. Many people avoid them entirely.
  • Research the team independently, and don't rely on links inside the project's own promotion.
  • Never invest more than you can afford to lose completely, and treat new tokens as extremely high risk.
  • Ignore hype from strangers and influencers. Paid promotion is common and often undisclosed.
  • Start with well-established assets if you decide to invest at all, and understand that even those carry serious risk.

If you think you've been rug pulled

  • Stop putting more money in, including "fees" to get out.
  • Save all evidence: token address, transaction IDs, website, chat logs.
  • Report it to the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov), the FTC (ReportFraud.ftc.gov), and the SEC (sec.gov/tcr).
  • Beware of anyone offering to "recover" the money for a fee. See How to Recover Stolen Crypto.

Keep in mind

  • New tokens can go to zero for many reasons, not only fraud.
  • Losses are usually permanent. There's no bank to reverse a trade.
  • No guarantee any check is enough. Even careful research can miss a determined scammer.

articles.title: Bitcoin vs. Ethereum: What's Actually Different?
articles.description: A side-by-side comparison of the two largest cryptocurrencies, in plain terms — what each one is actually for.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Written By the CryptoLearner Editorial Team
Last updated
Sep 2026

Why people compare them

Bitcoin and Ethereum are consistently the two largest cryptocurrencies by market value, so beginners naturally want to know how they differ. They share the same basic blockchain idea covered in How Does Cryptocurrency Actually Work?, but they were built with different goals.

What each one is actually for

AT A GLANCE
Bitcoin Ethereum
Launched 2009 2015
Main purpose A decentralized digital currency and store-of-value asset A programmable platform for running applications and "smart contracts"
Often compared to Digital gold A global, decentralized computer
Supply Fixed cap of 21 million coins No fixed hard cap
How new coins are added Mining (proof of work) Staking (proof of stake, since 2022)

What a "smart contract" actually is

Bitcoin's blockchain is mainly built to do one thing well: track ownership and transfers of bitcoin. Ethereum's blockchain was built to do much more, by allowing small programs, called smart contracts, to run directly on the network.

A smart contract is simply code that automatically carries out an agreement when certain conditions are met, without a company running it in the middle. For example, a smart contract could automatically swap one token for another the moment both sides deposit what they agreed to, with no bank or broker involved.

In plain terms

Bitcoin is closer to a specialized, secure ledger for one kind of money. Ethereum is closer to a shared computer that anyone can build applications on top of.

How each network agrees on what's true

Bitcoin uses proof of work, where computers compete using computing power to add new blocks, as explained in our blockchain guide. Ethereum originally used the same approach, but switched to proof of stake in 2022, an upgrade known as "the Merge."

Under proof of stake, participants lock up ETH as a deposit instead of competing with computing power, and can lose part of that deposit for dishonest behavior. Ethereum's move was driven partly by a goal of using significantly less energy than proof of work.

What people actually build or do on each

  • Bitcoin: primarily holding, transferring value, and using it as a long-term asset some investors compare to gold.
  • Ethereum: decentralized finance applications (lending, trading), NFTs, and a wide range of other applications built by independent developers, since anyone can build on the network.

This is why you'll often hear Ethereum described as an "ecosystem" rather than a single application, while Bitcoin stays deliberately narrower in scope by design.

Neither is inherently "better"

Comparisons often turn into arguments about which one will be worth more in the future. We won't make that argument, because nobody can honestly predict it. What's fair to say is that they were designed to solve different problems, and their trade-offs reflect that:

  • Bitcoin's narrow focus is often cited as a security strength, since there's less complexity to go wrong.
  • Ethereum's flexibility enables far more applications, but more code running on the network also means more opportunities for bugs or exploits in the applications built on it, not necessarily the base network itself.

Risks to understand

  • Both are highly volatile and have each fallen more than half from previous highs multiple times.
  • Neither has government insurance behind it.
  • Ethereum's flexibility adds layers of risk. Applications built on it can contain bugs or be exploited, separate from Ethereum itself.
  • Being "the largest" can change. Market rankings shift, and past dominance doesn't guarantee future performance.
  • Regulatory treatment may differ between the two and continues to evolve.

articles.title: Crypto has its own language. Here's the dictionary.
articles.description: Every industry develops its own shorthand, and crypto has more of it than most. This section is a running list of terms you'll run into everywhere else on this site (and across the internet), each explained in one or two plain sentences.
articles.author: cryptolearner.us Team
articles.content:
Sample entries

HODL

Crypto slang for holding onto an asset long-term instead of selling during price swings. Originally a misspelling of "hold" that stuck.

Blockchain

A shared, public record of transactions that many computers agree on together, instead of one central authority keeping the books.

Seed Phrase

A list of 12–24 random words that acts as the master password to a crypto wallet. Lose it, and there's usually no way to recover your funds.

Gas Fee

The cost charged to process a transaction on certain blockchains, similar in idea to a transaction or processing fee.

Market Cap

The total value of all coins of a given cryptocurrency in circulation — one basic way (not the only way) people compare the size of different coins.

Whitepaper

A document a crypto project publishes explaining what it does and how it works, similar to a business plan. Worth reading before trusting a claim about a coin.

Slippage

The difference between the price you expected for a trade and the price you actually got, usually caused by fast-moving markets.

Cold Wallet

A wallet that stores your crypto offline, disconnected from the internet, making it much harder to hack remotely.

This glossary is a living page — new terms are added as they come up across our guides. If you searched for a term and didn't find it here, use the "Talk to us" button and we'll add it.
